expurgate: Soften is far milder than expurgate — the rough joke stays in the text, just eased by a word or two, while expurgating strips the offending passages out entirely.
expurgate: Cut is stronger than soften but narrower than expurgate: you cut one scene, while expurgating means combing the whole work and stripping every part that could offend.
When the poet Ines Varga died in 1902, her sister Alba prepared the letters for publication — and prepared them thoroughly.
Alba expurgated the collection before the printer ever saw it, cutting every feud with a rival, every barbed remark about a critic, and every line about money.
The volume that appeared in 1904 was admired for its serenity; readers met a poet who seemed never to have quarreled with anyone.
A century later, scholars located the originals in a bank vault and printed them uncut.
Set side by side, the two editions tell different stories: one a monument, the other a life.

extant.definition: Extant means still existing, not destroyed or lost.
extant.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word extant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know extant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Of the balloon photographs taken over the city in 1906, eleven are extant, and nine of those show the same church.

Attested is a weaker claim than extant — a lost symphony known only from the printed program of its premiere is attested, nothing more; an extant work, however scorched or stained, still physically exists.
Intact goes further than extant: an extant manuscript may be a single scorched leaf, while an intact one has come through whole.

Surviving is the everyday word for what has come through when much around it was lost, and it fits people as naturally as papers. Extant is the scholar's ledger word for things — editions, specimens, recordings — that time has not yet destroyed, said when counting what remains.

Existing just means in being right now, with no story attached — existing rules, existing buildings. Extant carries the drama of the count: said of things time usually eats, it quietly reports that this particular one has not been destroyed or lost along the way.
gone as a kind, forever
disappeared, whereabouts unknown
Growers pay a premium to rent the cellar with the constant coolness.
Extant means still existing, not destroyed or lost.
Wax cylinders warp, crack, and grow mold, and the pianist died obscure; even her own label's vault ledger marks most titles destroyed.
Yet four cylinders are extant — two with collectors in Melbourne, one in a university basement, one found wedged inside a player sold at a farm auction.
The auction find, astonishingly, still plays.
Extant means still existing, not destroyed or lost, and it is said precisely of things time usually eats.
Note what the word does not claim: condition.
An extant cylinder may be cracked past playing — extant reports only that the thing itself has not vanished from the world.
Extant is catalog language — editions, specimens, recordings, buildings — and it often follows its noun ("three copies are extant").

Use surviving in ordinary prose; reach for extant when counting what time has spared, and note the contrast baked into its antonym: a species is extinct, but the two museum skins of it are, strangely, still extant.

Against that arithmetic, the archive's new catalogue reads like a rescue log.
For each title it records one word where it matters most: extant.
The entry does not promise beauty.
An extant film may be one reel of five, water-spotted, missing its ending.
It promises something narrower and better: the thing itself still physically exists, somewhere, on a shelf a researcher can visit.
Titles known only from posters and newspaper advertisements get a different, sadder label, and a separate list.

extol.definition: Extol means to praise enthusiastically — to lift something up in words, warmly and at full voice.
extol.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word extol. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know extol should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Coach Imani spends the first practice extolling the humble hill sprint, promising her freshmen it will repay every groan they give it.
Commend is milder than extol: a commendation notes merit in a sentence and stops, while extolling settles in — praise built point by point, at full voice.
Glorify is stronger than extol: extolling praises a real thing for real virtues, while glorifying inflates past the evidence, polishing its subject toward the mythic.
To laud is to praise formally, often on the record — a citation lauds. Extol shares the formality but adds fervor and push: extolling praises at length, virtue by virtue, to win the listener over.
To tout is to promote something loudly, often with an eye on the sale — the pitch matters more than the truth. Extol praises just as loudly but in earnest: an extoller believes every word.
to talk something down as minor or worthless
to make something sound smaller and less impressive than it is
Her roommate can tolerate almost anything except a dish left overnight in the sink — that, and only that, convenes a house meeting.
Extol means to praise enthusiastically — to lift something up in words, warmly and at full voice.
At the co-op's annual meeting, the produce manager stood to extol the ugly carrots — knobbly, cheap, and twice as sweet — until the board voted to double the order.
Extolling is praise with a pulpit and a purpose: the manager doesn't just like the carrots, he lifts them up before an audience, virtue by virtue, to move that audience to act.
That upward, out-loud push is the word's whole gesture — you extol in words, and always toward other ears.
Extol is praise on its feet, making a case: you extol to move an audience — a committee, a crowd, a readership.
Its unit-mates divide the territory: exalt raises its subject's rank, acclaim is the applause coming back, and rhapsodize gushes for the pleasure of gushing.
Extol works when the praise has a purpose; nobody extols quietly, and nobody extols by accident.

Instead the chef spends them extolling her favorite vegetable, point by point: its price, its patience in a cold cellar, the seven distinct textures she insists it contains, its centuries of quiet service in a dozen cuisines.
The tone is not salesmanship — she has nothing to gain; cabbage is not sponsoring anyone — but conviction at full volume.
Reviewers admit the praise is contagious.
'By page thirty,' one wrote, 'I had put down the book, gone out, and bought three heads of it.' The recipes, when they finally arrive, feel almost like an afterthought.

extraneous.definition: Extraneous means irrelevant, extra, not necessary.
extraneous.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word extraneous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know extraneous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Log only the pendulum's swing time, the lab sheet warns; the color of the string is extraneous data.
An unneeded detail merely fails to help; an extraneous one comes from outside the subject entirely — it was never part of the matter to begin with.
Distracting sits a rung past extraneous: the imported material has stopped being harmless and started pulling attention away from the point.

Irrelevant judges a thing against the question at hand: whatever it is and wherever it came from, it fails to bear on the point. Extraneous adds a story about origin — the material walked in from outside the subject entirely. A detail can be irrelevant while still belonging to the file; extraneous detail never belonged.

Unrelated is the total break: the thing has no connection to the matter at all, near or far. Extraneous is softer and more particular — extraneous material can touch the subject and still not belong, because it was imported from somewhere else. Everything unrelated is extraneous; not the reverse.
bearing directly on the matter
belonging naturally to the discussion at hand
Astronomers scan the sky for radio signals that might carry an extraterrestrial hello.
Extraneous means irrelevant, extra, not necessary.
The volcano-acidity poster lost points for its extraneous panels: a timeline of the student's pets, a photo of the family dog wearing safety goggles, and a paragraph on favorite lunches.
Charming, every one — and none of it had anything to do with volcanoes.
Extraneous is the precise word because the material comes from outside the subject.
The dog photo isn't wrong, sloppy, or false; it simply doesn't belong to the matter at hand.
Extraneous marks that outsider status — imported material a subject never asked for.
Extraneous and superfluous — a unit-mate — divide the territory of 'too much.' Extraneous material comes from outside the subject: the pet timeline on a volcano poster.
Superfluous material belongs in kind but exceeds the need: the fourth example proving a point the first three settled.
Off-topic, reach for extraneous; on-topic but past need, superfluous.

The conservator's first task with the harbor painting was subtraction.
Under ultraviolet light, whole passages glowed a different age: a lighthouse, two gulls, and a band of dramatic cloud, none painted by the original artist.
A dealer had added them a century later to suit Victorian taste.
However pretty, they were extraneous — imported onto a canvas they were never part of.
The original varnish line ran beneath them, unbroken, like a floor under later furniture.
Solvent by solvent, the additions lifted away, and the painter's own bare, quiet harbor came back.

extrapolate.definition: Extrapolate means to extend known information beyond its last point to estimate what is unknown.
extrapolate.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word extrapolate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know extrapolate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Census planners extrapolate a county's population from the handful of blocks they can actually visit.
To infer is milder than to extrapolate: an inference rests directly on the evidence in front of you, while extrapolation stretches that evidence out past its edge.
Conjecture goes further than extrapolate — it leaps with hardly any data at all, where extrapolation at least follows a measured trend.

Project runs current numbers forward — the business-page cousin of extrapolate. A treasurer projects next quarter's revenue from this quarter's books. Extrapolate is the broader, more technical move: extending any measured trend past its last data point, whether the data is money, votes, or rainfall.

Forecast predicts what is coming, in weather-report register — a forecast of storms, of turnout, of demand. It names the prediction, not the method. Extrapolate names the method itself: stretch the trend you measured past its final point and read off where it lands.
to read the value directly instead of estimating it
to count exactly what is in front of you, nothing beyond

From the first hour of early voting — forty ballots, a steady line — the county clerk extrapolated the whole day's turnout, called two retired poll workers before lunch, and had extra chairs and a second scanner in place for the afternoon rush.
Extrapolate fits because the clerk stretched a measured trend past its last data point: one hour, extended to twelve.
Infer would cover any conclusion drawn from evidence; predict says nothing about method.
Extrapolate names the specific move — and its specific risk, since a trend may bend after the sample ends.
Extrapolate belongs to graphs, budgets, and forecasts — extending a known trend past its last data point.
Where the unknown lies between known points, the word is interpolate; where there is no trend at all, you are only guessing.

In 1954, plenty of physiologists insisted the four-minute mile sat at the very edge of human ability.
A statistician saw it differently.
Record times had been falling by nearly a second a year for three decades, and he simply let the line keep going.
To extrapolate from the trend was not to promise anything -- it was to say that if the curve held, a 3:58 would arrive within a few years.
The method has famous failures too.
Stretch the same line far enough and it predicts a two-minute mile, which no amount of training will ever deliver.
The lesson runners' statisticians repeat: data earns you the next step past its edge, and no more.
The farther beyond your last measurement you reach, the thinner the ground.

extricate.definition: Extricate means to disentangle or free from something.
extricate.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word extricate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know extricate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Rosa spent half the reception extricating herself from a conversation that restarted every time she edged toward the door.
Loosen is far milder than extricate — the grip eases a little, but the thing is still caught; to extricate is to work it all the way free.
Release is milder than extricate: it simply lets go, while extricating means working something free from a snarl that fights back.

Free is the plain, all-purpose word for letting something go, and it implies no struggle at all. Extricate earns its extra syllables only when the freeing takes work: something tangled, wedged, or trapped has to be worked loose against real resistance.

Disentangle keeps its eyes on the tangle itself — undoing the knots and loops, strand by strand. Extricate looks at the captive instead: you extricate the drone, the driver, or yourself from whatever holds on, with patience and effort.
snarl something up in loops and knots
trap something deliberately
The ambassador's memoir promises a chapter on the intrigue that cost her predecessor his post.
Extricate means to disentangle or free from something.
The drone came down in a kite-flying park, and the club's youngest member spent an hour on a ladder extricating it, easing the tangled line off one rotor at a time until the machine lifted free.
Extricate is more precise than free or remove because it implies a real entanglement and careful work — the drone was not simply picked up but worked loose from a snarl that resisted.
Extricate earns its length when the freeing takes work — rescue crews extricate drivers, lawyers extricate clients, and you extricate yourself from an awkward promise.
If nothing resisted, plain free or remove is honest.
The word keeps its picture of tangles, so it pairs naturally with nets, wreckage, red tape, and long conversations.

Midway through the regional robotics final, the Hawthorne team's rover wedged itself under a fallen ramp, one wheel jammed in the frame and a cable snagged on a bolt.
The rules allowed a single rescue: two students could enter the arena and extricate the machine, but the clock would keep running the whole time.
Watching rivals lose a minute to panic, the Hawthorne pair moved slowly instead.
They unhooked the cable first, then rocked the chassis backward until the wheel came clear of the frame.
It cost them ninety seconds, and the judges made no adjustment for the mishap.
But the rover finished its run, and the team took second place — proof, their coach said, that patient hands beat quick ones when a machine has to be worked out of a trap.

exult.definition: Exult means to rejoice openly and at full volume — triumphant joy let out in leaps and shouts.
exult.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word exult. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know exult should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The moment her visa approval loaded on the screen, Amara exulted — one enormous whoop that startled the whole internet cafe.
A smile is joy at its quietest — barely a ripple next to exulting.
A cheer is one burst of voiced joy; exulting is louder and longer than a cheer — whole-body celebration that refuses to sit down.

To rejoice is the plain, hymnal word for gladness — it can be quiet, inward, even solemn. To exult is rejoicing with the lid off: loud, physical, and unmistakable, triumph that leaps and shouts. A congregation can rejoice in silence; nobody exults in silence.

To crow is to exult a little too loudly and at somebody — boasting over a beaten rival with a rooster's tact. Exulting is joy aimed at the sky; crowing aims it at the loser. A team may exult all night with perfect grace and never crow once.
to grieve a loss
to give up hope entirely
The gymnast finished with a double somersault and stuck the landing to a roar.
Exult means to rejoice openly and at full volume — triumphant joy let out in leaps and shouts.
After six dense, doorstop failures, the seventh loaf rose — and Marco exulted, parading it around the kitchen on its cutting board like a championship belt.
To exult is to let triumph out — loud, physical, unmistakable rejoicing.
It is intransitive: you exult, or exult in a victory, or exult over a rival's stumble (a shading that borders on gloating).
Its look-alike exalt (this unit) aims praise at someone else; exult is joy aimed at the sky.
Exult when joy goes public — winning teams exult, rescued crews exult, grandmothers exult at spelling bees.
It is grander than celebrate and louder than rejoice.
Mind the twin: exult is your own leaping joy; exalt (this unit) lifts someone else onto the pedestal.

For three rounds the Jefferson Middle robotics team had been the picture of composure, whispering over schematics while their robot, Beatrice, stacked blocks with surgical calm.
Then the final buzzer sounded, the scores posted, and composure went out the window.
The team exulted the way only twelve-year-olds can: leaping over pit tables, waving foam wrenches, roaring Beatrice's name until the announcer gave up talking over them.
Notably, none of it was aimed at the second-place team, who got handshakes and, eventually, help carrying their crates to the bus.

The ceiling seemed like the right audience.'

fable.definition: A fable is a short, openly invented tale that teaches a lesson — often through talking animals — and, by extension, any account that is invention rather than fact.
fable.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Grandfather passed it off as family history, but the tale of the wolf who guarded our orchard is pure fable — no wolf, no orchard, just a lesson about patience he wanted us to keep.
An anecdote is milder stuff than a fable: one small moment offered as true, nothing invented and nothing to prove — a fable invents freely and aims its whole tale at a single lesson.
Myth goes further than fable: a fable spends its invention on one compact lesson, while a myth swells to carry a people's entire picture of the world — origins, gods, and all.

A parable teaches through lifelike, everyday people — two debtors, a lost sheep, a quarrel over a well — events that could happen on any street. A fable announces its invention from the first line: talking beasts, impossible bargains, a tale nobody was ever meant to believe.

A yarn is a long, colorful story spun mainly for the fun of the telling, and it sprawls wherever the teller wanders. A fable is compact and aimed: every invented detail exists to deliver the one lesson waiting at the end.
a plain, dated record of what actually happened
testimony bound to what was really seen
Fans lingered at the affable shortstop's locker long after the loss, and even the beat writers went home smiling.
A fable is a short, openly invented tale that teaches a lesson — often through talking animals — and, by extension, any account that is invention rather than fact.
In the sailors' fable, a gull trades her wings to a fish for a coat of silver scales — and spends the rest of the tale sinking slowly, wishing back what she gave away.
No one who tells it thinks a gull ever made such a bargain, and that is the point.

A fable does not ask to be believed: it is invention worn openly, animals doing impossible things so that the lesson underneath — what you surrender to become what you envy — can be handed over without an argument.

Fable is a genre label first — Aesop's talking foxes — but English also uses it dismissively, for any account that is invention wearing the clothes of fact: 'the numbers in the prospectus were pure fable.' Its neighbors divide the storytelling work: a parable keeps to lifelike, everyday people; a legend attaches itself to a real name or place and grows in the telling; a myth expands to explain a people's whole world.
In this unit's spirit, remember the dismissive sense — calling a report a fable is a polite way of calling it false.

Every schoolchild knows the fable: the ant works all summer, the grasshopper fiddles, and winter settles the argument.
The entomologist Elena Ruiz has spent a career being mildly annoyed by it.
Real grasshoppers, she points out, do not starve for laziness — most species simply die before winter, industrious or not, and no amount of summer prudence would save them.
But she concedes the story was never about insects.
Its talking idlers and smug workers exist to hand children a lesson about planning, and the entomology is beside the point.
That, she tells her students, is the bargain such tales make: they lie freely about the world in order to say one true thing about us.

fabricate.definition: Fabricate means to invent something and present it as real.
fabricate.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fabricate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fabricate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The salesman fabricated a waiting list, quoting names and dates to buyers who never suspected the ledger page was empty.
Misstate is the mildest rung, far below fabricate — a misstated figure gets one thing wrong, sometimes not even on purpose.
Doctor stops short of fabricate: to doctor a report is to tamper with something real, while to fabricate is to build the entire thing from nothing.

To invent is to create something new — a machine or a lie with equal ease, and the word itself passes no judgment. Fabricate narrows invention to deception: a fabricated record is built piece by piece and presented as real, and the accusation is always deliberate.

To forge is to fake a specific document or signature, producing a counterfeit passed off as genuine. Fabricate is wider — a whole alibi, career, or past can be fabricated — and it points at the deliberate construction, not the imitation of someone else's paperwork.
admit what really happened

The tailor tested the fabric by holding it up against the window light.
Fabricate means to invent something and present it as real.

Fabricate comes from the workshop: it means to build.
A fabricated alibi, résumé, or record is manufactured — constructed piece by piece and presented as real.
Concocting is quicker and looser; fabricating implies deliberate construction, often with props to show.
Fabricate is the investigator's verb — evidence, records, and résumés get fabricated, and the word implies deliberate construction.
Concoct, in this same unit, is its quicker, flimsier cousin, thrown together on the spot.
For paperwork faked in someone else's name, forge is more exact.

For sixty years the Hargrove diary anchored the museum's Civil War room, its pages quoted in textbooks and read aloud on anniversaries.
Then a graduate student noticed the paper was machine-made, a stock not milled until decades after the war.
Chemists confirmed her suspicion: the ink, the binding, even the water stains were modern.
The museum's own founder, it now appears, had fabricated the diary in 1921 — composing the entries himself, staining the pages with tea, and presenting the whole volume as a soldier's testimony.
Nothing in it records a life; every line was manufactured to be believed.

facetious.definition: Facetious means treating a serious matter with inappropriate humor; not meant to be taken seriously.
facetious.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word facetious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know facetious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Asked on the evacuation form to list a meeting point, Theo wrote 'the moon' — a facetious answer his RA made him redo on the spot.
Playful is milder than facetious — playful humor suits the moment it lands in, while facetious humor barges in where seriousness belongs.
Flippant goes further than facetious — a facetious answer jokes when it should be serious, while a flippant one signals that the speaker doesn't respect the matter at all.

Joking just means playing for laughs, and it is neutral about the setting — a joking toast at a party is perfectly welcome. Facetious is the charged version: joking aimed where seriousness belongs, the gag offered in place of the real answer a moment requires.

Tongue-in-cheek humor is ironic by design — the speaker says one thing, means another, and trusts the audience to catch the wink. Facetious needs no irony: it marks any joke, plain or coded, dropped where a serious answer was owed. The offense in facetious is the timing, not the wink.
meaning what you say, treating the matter with weight
gravely formal, without any lightness at all

facile.definition: Facile means superficial; achieved with too little thought or care.
facile.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word facile. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know facile should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The seminar's rule, posted on the door, was that facile answers — the ones that fit on a bumper sticker — earn a follow-up question.
A pat answer is suspiciously neat — rehearsed-sounding, a little too smooth — but pat stays milder than facile: pat may still be true, while facile means the thinking was skipped.
Hollow goes further than facile — the facile argument is thin but holds something; the hollow one collapses at the first press.

Shallow measures depth and nothing else: little lies beneath the surface, whether of a person, a friendship, or an idea. Facile points at the workmanship — an answer achieved with too little thought, its surface appeal intact. Shallow describes what a thing is; facile blames how it was made.

Glib describes a speaker — fluent, quick, and persuasive on the surface, with the thought missing underneath. Facile judges the product instead: the argument or fix achieved with too little care. A glib salesman talks past hard questions; a facile plan simply never met one.
digging past the first answer
the work actually done, corner to corner
The wider loading door facilitated the piano's move into the studio.

fallacious.definition: Fallacious means based on unsound or misleading reasoning.
fallacious.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fallacious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fallacious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: His proof that the team wins whenever he wears the lucky socks is fallacious—the team also wins plenty of games while the socks stay home.
A shaky argument has weak spots a good editor might shore up; a fallacious one is built on a genuine logical flaw and cannot stand as reasoned.
Incoherent lies beyond fallacious: a fallacious argument at least hangs together well enough to fool someone, while an incoherent one offers no recognizable chain of reasoning at all.

Illogical means the steps of thinking go wrong — a conclusion that does not follow, a rule of sense broken along the way — and it can be entirely innocent. Fallacious adds a misleading edge: the flawed reasoning is dressed up to persuade, built well enough to take in a careless reader.

Unsound means resting on a defective foundation, whether the flaw sits in the facts or in the logic — a bridge design and an argument can both be unsound. Fallacious is the narrower verdict: the reasoning itself is broken, however true the individual facts may be.
built on solid evidence and correct steps
correctly reasoned, with conclusions that follow from the premises

Fallacious means based on unsound or misleading reasoning.

Fallacious is not the same as 'false': the speaker might even turn out to be a great inventor.
The word condemns the argument, not the conclusion—the logic is broken no matter how things end.
Fallacious is a precision tool for arguments and reasoning—essays, editorials, proofs.

At the regional science fair, the most confident poster belonged to a student who had played classical music to one tray of bean seedlings.
The music tray grew taller, the poster announced, therefore music makes beans grow.
A judge stopped and read it twice.
Her scorecard called the conclusion fallacious, and she was careful about the word: the measurements were accurate and neatly recorded.
The problem was the reasoning built on them.
The music tray also sat beside the window, so sunlight, not sound, could explain everything.
The argument looked persuasive, she wrote, and that was exactly the trouble -- it invited you to skip the step that failed.

falsifiable.definition: Falsifiable means able to be proven wrong by evidence or observation.
falsifiable.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word falsifiable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know falsifiable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her claim that the cat opens the pantry at night is falsifiable: one cheap camera on the shelf settles it either way.
An arguable claim can be batted back and forth with reasons forever, and no round of debate ever finishes it; a falsifiable claim is braver — it points to evidence that could end the matter for good.
A testable claim lets some evidence bear on it; falsifiable is the strictest rung — it names the exact result that would prove the claim dead wrong.

Disprovable is falsifiable's plain-English twin: evidence could show the claim is wrong. Falsifiable is the laboratory's version of the same virtue and adds the emphasis scientists prize — the claim itself spells out, in advance, exactly which observation would kill it.

Refutable belongs to the debate hall: a refutable claim can be knocked down with arguments, counterexamples, and logic. Falsifiable moves the contest outdoors — it is settled by observation rather than rhetoric, and the falsifiable claim names the measurement or find that would prove it wrong.
too hazy for any evidence to pin down
beyond disproof — no evidence could count against it
The tenor slid into falsetto for the final note, and the hall went silent.
Falsifiable means able to be proven wrong by evidence or observation.
The bridge foreman's boast — 'this deck will not flex more than a centimeter under a fully loaded train' — is falsifiable in the most literal way.
Mount a gauge, run the train, read the needle: past one centimeter, the boast dies on the spot.

Falsifiable is praise in science's own tongue: a claim brave enough to name what would prove it wrong.
The centimeter boast stakes itself on a needle; the 'triumph' line risks nothing and so, to a scientist, says nothing.

Falsifiable is a term of praise in laboratories: a claim honest enough to name its own kill switch.

fastidious.definition: Fastidious means extremely exacting and hard to please about details.
fastidious.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fastidious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fastidious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Our fastidious neighbor hoses down her recycling before sorting it by color, then by lid.
A particular eater has likes and states them; a fastidious one sends the plate back over the parsley.
Obsessive goes past fastidious — the checking never ends, long after every box has been ticked.

Picky is fastidious in street clothes — the everyday word for the same impossible-to-please fussiness, aimed mostly at choices: toppings sent back, seats swapped, brands refused. Fastidious dresses the trait for formal use and points it at standards and details rather than menus.

Exacting describes the demand itself: a standard set high and enforced, usually on other people's work — the exacting editor requires every rule kept. Fastidious describes the temperament behind such demands, hard to please past reason; meet the exacting bar and you are done, while the fastidious eye keeps hunting.
content with however things turn out

An actress once changed a button backstage; Duval spotted it from the wings at forty feet.

fatalistic.definition: Fatalistic means convinced that events are decided by fate and cannot be changed.
fatalistic.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fatalistic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fatalistic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Dario was fatalistic about auditions: 'They cast the part before you walk in,' he would shrug, 'so you might as well walk in relaxed.'
Passive people simply don't act — a milder condition than fatalistic, which supplies the reason no one should bother: the outcome is already written.
Nihilistic goes further than fatalistic: fatalism says the ending is fixed, nihilism says there was never any meaning in the story at all.

A defeatist is braced to lose this particular fight — the match, the election, the audit — and behaves as if the loss has already happened. Fatalistic runs wider and deeper: it says every outcome, wins included, was scripted in advance. A defeatist expects to lose; a fatalistic person expects nothing anyone does to matter.

Hopeless means without hope of any good outcome — the future looks dark from every angle. Fatalistic is not about darkness but about authorship: a fatalistic person may cheerfully expect good things, believing only that fate, never effort, will deliver them. Hopeless despairs of the ending; fatalistic just hands over the steering wheel.

Fatalistic means convinced that events are decided by fate and cannot be changed.

Fatalistic is more precise than 'gloomy' or 'negative' because it names a belief, not a mood: that events are decided in advance and effort cannot bend them.
A fatalistic person can even be cheerful — they've simply stopped believing that trying changes anything.

Weddings on the Point are loud, and the boats are painted in carnival colors.

fathom.definition: Fathom means to understand something deeply — to get to the bottom of it.
fathom.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fathom. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fathom should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Naval historians still cannot fathom why the flagship turned into the storm when every signal ordered her home.
To follow an argument is just to keep up with it step by step — far short of fathoming it.
To grasp an idea stops short of fathoming it: you hold the main point, but the bottom is still out of reach.

Comprehend is the formal word for full understanding — a reader comprehends a passage and can restate its point. Fathom digs further down and usually appears in the negative: to fathom something is to reach its very bottom, which is exactly what keeps failing when the word shows up.

Decipher means to decode something hidden — bad handwriting, a cipher, a garbled signal — and once decoded it turns plain. Fathom needs nothing decoded: the thing sits in plain sight, and what resists you is its depth. You decipher a coded note; you fathom why it was written.
to take the wrong meaning from what's in front of you
to mix ideas up instead of making sense of them

Fathom is Old English faethm, the span of two outstretched arms — about six feet. Sailors measured depth by paying out rope one arm-span at a time, so 'to fathom' became to reach the very bottom of a thing. No other English word descends from it.
Fathom means to understand something deeply — to get to the bottom of it.
Rosa could not fathom the appeal of the mobile game her roommates played for hours — she tapped the same three buttons they did and felt nothing but the minutes leaving.
Fathom digs deeper than 'understand': an old sailor's word for sounding the sea's depth, it means getting all the way to the bottom of something — which is why it usually appears when someone can't.
neutral, usually in the negative

For ordinary comprehension, 'grasp' or 'follow' will do; fathom promises the very bottom of the thing.

fatuous.definition: Fatuous means smugly foolish; silly and empty of sense.
fatuous.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fatuous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fatuous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The talk show fills its last segment with fatuous predictions delivered in sober confidence — last week a guest guaranteed weather control by June.

Witless means empty of intelligence — no thought at work anywhere in the remark or the plan — and it passes no judgment on the speaker's mood. Fatuous needs one thing more: the glow of self-congratulation. Witless names the vacancy; fatuous is the vacancy taking a bow.

The family let the subject drift out with the tide.

fecund.definition: Fecund means fertile, producing new life or ideas in teeming abundance.
fecund.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fecund. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fecund should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The volcanic terraces are so fecund that farmers there joke about harvesting anything they happen to drop.
Productive stops short of fecund — a productive plot meets its quota and not much more.
Fruitful stops short of fecund — a fruitful season gives a good yield, while a fecund one buries you in zucchini and volunteer seedlings.

Prolific counts the output: a prolific author, a prolific vine — many works, many grapes, one after another. Fecund points at the generative power behind the output, the teeming fertility that keeps producing whether anyone asks or not. Bountiful praises what is given — a bountiful harvest, a bountiful host — generosity in the yield itself. Fecund looks earlier in the process, at the power to keep producing: soil, species, or minds teeming with new life. A bountiful table is loaded once; a fecund garden keeps loading it.

Fecund arrived whole from Latin fecundus, 'fruitful.' Its ancient root — meaning 'to nourish, to suckle' — does survive, but only in remote technical words like fetus, which no longer look or feel related. With no everyday cousin to give it away, fecund must be learned on its own.

fickle.definition: Fickle means changing often and without warning.

Its finale drew record numbers; its catchphrases covered lunchboxes and bumper stickers.
Then, without any scandal or slump in quality, the audience simply moved on — ratings fell by half in a spring, and the lunchboxes went to clearance.
Critics shrugged and reached for an old word: audiences are fickle, they wrote, and adoration is a lease, never a deed.
The network's new hit, a pottery contest, is enjoying the same devotion now.
Its producers, reading history, have declined to celebrate.

figurative.definition: Figurative means expressing meaning through imagery rather than literal statement.
figurative.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word figurative. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know figurative should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Nobody at the seed store believed the tomatoes truly drink sunshine, and the clerk's figurative pitch still sold out the flat by noon.
Vivid is milder than figurative — vivid wording paints sharply but can stay perfectly literal; a vivid fact is still a fact.
Fantastical goes further than figurative: figurative language borrows an image while meaning something real, but the fantastical leaves reality behind altogether.

Metaphorical names one specific move: speaking through one thing to mean another, as when a deadline 'looms' or a rumor 'spreads like wildfire.' Figurative is the umbrella over that move and its cousins — simile, hyperbole, personification. Every metaphorical phrase is figurative; not every figurative phrase is a metaphor.

Symbolic points at objects and images set up to stand for something beyond themselves — a dove for peace, a broken clock for lost time. Figurative describes wording instead: language that trades literal statement for imagery. A symbol sits in the scene; figurative language lives in the phrasing.
meaning exactly what the words state

The vandals who disfigured the fountain were caught on the library's cameras by nightfall.

When the news anchor says the river 'shrugged off' the new levee, she speaks in images: rivers have no shoulders, but the borrowed shrug captures what the footage showed — water moving past the barrier as if it were not there.
That is figurative speech at work.
Figurative is the umbrella term for meaning carried by imagery instead of literal statement — and it is not a polite word for false.
The water really did move past; only the shrug was borrowed.
If every element of a whole work carries a second meaning, you have moved past figurative language into allegory.
Figurative is the wide, workhorse label: any wording that trades literal statement for imagery.

The town was hot, the mosquitoes were thick; the oven and the sparrows were just her way of making him feel it.
That June, Tomas wrote back in kind, reporting that his summer reading list had 'swallowed the living room.'

figurehead.definition: Figurehead means a leader in title only, without real power.
figurehead.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word figurehead. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know figurehead should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Everyone photographs the parade marshal waving from the lead car, but the marshal is a figurehead; the parade office plans every float and street closure.
A deputy already outranks a figurehead where it counts: the deputy's power is borrowed, but it is real, while the figurehead's grand title commands nothing.
The autocrat stands at the ladder's far end from the figurehead: every decision in the realm flows from the autocrat personally, while the figurehead decides nothing at all.

A puppet is a leader actively operated by someone hidden behind him: the strings are pulled, the lines are fed, the decisions arrive pre-made. A figurehead is emptier but freer — the title carries no power, yet no one is working him. A figurehead is left alone with an empty title; a puppet never is.

A mouthpiece exists to deliver someone else's words aloud — a spokesperson reading the official line — and claims no leadership of his own. flabbergasted.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word flabbergasted. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know flabbergasted should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The plumber cut into the kitchen wall to trace a leak and stood flabbergasted: behind the plaster ran a painted 1920s mural, intact from floor to ceiling.
Surprised is the everyday word — an unexpected knock surprises you — and it sits far below flabbergasted.
Astonished goes further than surprised, striking real wonder, but it stops short of flabbergasted, which leaves you gaping with nothing to say.

Dumbfounded zooms in on one symptom of shock: the words stop coming, and you stand there with nothing to say. Flabbergasted names the whole state — utterly astounded by something almost past believing. A hard riddle can leave you dumbfounded; flabbergasted needs real news, a jaw-dropper that upends what you thought you knew.

Stunned means knocked briefly out of the ability to react — by news or by a blow — so that for a moment you cannot respond. Flabbergasted is bigger and louder: utterly astounded by something you can scarcely believe. A stunned person freezes for a beat; a flabbergasted one can hardly accept what just happened.

Flabbergast arrived as ready-made slang in the 1770s — a London magazine listed it among the year's new vogue words — and whatever was mashed together to coin it was never written down. It has no traceable root and therefore no cousins; the word stands alone.
Flabbergasted means utterly astounded.

The room sat flabbergasted — forks down, mouths open — for a long moment before the applause hit.
Flabbergasted is far stronger than 'surprised': it means utterly astounded, knocked right past speech.
You are surprised by a pop quiz; you are flabbergasted when the quiz is handed out by the superintendent, in costume, on live television.
Flabbergasted is conversational and a little theatrical — perfect in speech and light prose for total astonishment.

The painting sold for enough to reroof the barn twice over, and Harlan says he still does not quite believe the number.

flaccid.definition: Flaccid means completely loose and floppy — lacking the firmness or strength something is supposed to have.
flaccid.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word flaccid. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know flaccid should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Flaccid means limp and soft — lacking the firmness something should have, like a balloon three days after the party, hanging flaccid and wrinkled from its ribbon.
Soft things yield to pressure but can still hold their shape; flaccid things have lost their firmness completely and droop.
Lifeless goes beyond flaccid — a flaccid stem still has some substance to it, but a lifeless one has nothing left at all.

Limp means without stiffness or firmness right now — a limp handshake, limp lettuce, limp noodles. It is the everyday word. Flaccid means the same physical looseness but sounds clinical and precise, the term a doctor or gardener might use for muscles or stems that have lost their firmness.

Droopy describes things hanging or sagging downward weakly — droopy eyelids, a droopy houseplant. It is about posture: which way something sags. Flaccid is about internal firmness being gone entirely, whatever position the thing is in. A droopy flower bends over; a flaccid stem has no firmness left inside.

Floppy means loose and bending easily — describing things that visibly flop about when moved, like a hat brim, a puppy's ears, or an old paperback's cover. It is casual and a little playful. Flaccid is its clinical cousin: the formal word for tissue or material that has lost the firmness it should have.
solid and holding its shape

flagrant.definition: Flagrant means offensive, egregious; glaringly bad.
flagrant.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word flagrant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know flagrant should be able to work it out from your sentence.

Blatant stops a step short of flagrant: both are impossible to miss, but flagrant adds the offense — a blatant hint is loud, a flagrant foul is loud and wrong.

Glaring means impossible to overlook — a glaring error announces itself from across the room. It measures visibility alone. Flagrant measures visibility and guilt at once: a flagrant violation is both unmissable and inexcusable, while a glaring one may be an innocent mistake.

flatten.definition: Flatten means to make something flat, so that whatever had height loses it.
flatten.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word flatten. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know flatten should be able to work it out from your sentence.

Smooth does much less than flatten — it only erases the surface's ridges while the shape underneath keeps its height; flattening presses the whole shape down toward level.

Level aims at evenness — a graded road, a floor, a playing field brought to one height. Flatten names a loss instead: whatever had height gives it up entirely. You can level a bumpy lawn and it is still a lawn; flatten a hedge and its shape is gone.

Squash is the informal, kitchen-floor word: flatness produced by sudden force, a grape under a heel. Flatten is calmer and more general — you can flatten a box slowly and neatly, on purpose, and what is flattened survives as a tidy sheet rather than a burst mess.

The print shop's oldest machine is a hand-cranked press, and its whole job is pressure.
Fresh paper arrives with a slight wave to it, so the printers flatten each stack first, leaving it under iron weights overnight until every sheet lies as thin and true as the tabletop.
Nothing about the step is violent.
The weights come down slowly, the paper survives in perfect condition, and by morning the stack has simply given up its height.
Visitors sometimes ask why the crew bothers, since the paper already looks fine at a glance.
The foreman's answer never changes: ink forgives many sins, but it will not forgive a sheet that still remembers its curl.

fleeting.definition: Fleeting means lasting only an instant and gone before you can hold it — over almost as soon as it is noticed.

Passing is weaker than fleeting — a passing mood can take a whole afternoon to move through, while a fleeting one is gone in the space of a glance.
Evanescent is stronger than fleeting — a fleeting moment at least arrives whole before it goes, while an evanescent one is already dissolving as it appears, like breath on cold glass.

What the bay offers is fleeting: a fin for half a breath, a spout already dissolving by the time a hand can rise to aim a phone.

The second, a girl in a yellow coat saw the whole arc — and caught none of it on camera.

florid.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word florid. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know florid should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: His thank-you note ran two florid pages when one plain sentence would have done.
Fancy is a few dressy touches — it stops well short of florid.
Overwrought goes further than florid: the ornament turns to strain, every line overloaded past bearing.

Flowery is the everyday word for dressed-up language, and it is the gentler charge — a few blossoms too many. Florid is stronger and more formal: the whole style is in full ornamental flower, decoration crowding out substance line after line.

High-flown language reaches upward — grand, lofty phrases straining to sound important. Florid decorates instead: curls, blossoms, and perfumed flourishes laid over the sentence. A high-flown speech aims too high; a florid one is dressed too richly, and a passage can easily be both.
saying it simply, without ornament
deliberately quieter than it could be
Critics date the movement's efflorescence to a single Paris season.
Florid means flowery, ornate.
The listing described a modest bungalow in florid prose — 'a jewel-box sanctuary bathed in dawn's first amber' — and the buyers who pulled up to the plain little porch felt swindled by adjectives.
Florid is more exact than 'wordy' because the problem isn't length, it's decoration: the sentence is dressed in curls and blossoms of language.
A long plain paragraph is merely wordy; ten words wearing perfume and lace are florid.
Florid is mostly for style — speech, prose, lettering, music — and it usually carries a raised eyebrow: decoration has gotten ahead of substance.
Its neighbor ornate does the same work for physical objects (an ornate frame, a florid speech), and garish adds the charge of clashing bad taste.
Florid can also describe a flushed red complexion; that older sense is worth recognizing on sight.

forsake.definition: Forsake means to give up or renounce something one is attached to.
forsake.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word forsake. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know forsake should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Offered a larger parish in the capital, the young priest chose not to forsake the mountain village that had raised him.
Drop is far milder than forsake — you drop a hobby the way you drop a habit, and nobody mourns; to forsake is to give up something loved, and the loss aches.
Abandon is milder than forsake even so: you can abandon a broken umbrella without a flicker, while forsake carries the ache of leaving something loved.

Desert means to walk out on someone or something that counts on you — a post, a family, a crew — and it points hard at the betrayal. Forsake points at the attachment instead: what is forsaken was loved, and the word carries the ache of the parting.

hold something dear and keep it close

forthright.definition: Forthright means direct and honest in what one says.
forthright.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word forthright. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know forthright should be able to work it out from your sentence.

Tactless goes further than forthright and falls off the good end of the ladder: the forthright speaker tells hard truths with care, while the tactless one tramples feelings without noticing.

Outspoken people voice their opinions freely and unprompted, sometimes more often and more loudly than anyone asked. Forthright is narrower: it means answering what you are asked directly and honestly. The outspoken volunteer their views; the forthright deliver the truth a question was owed.

fortitude.definition: Fortitude means strength of mind in facing danger, pain, or adversity; courage under strain.
fortitude.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fortitude. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fortitude should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: It took real fortitude for the rookie reporter to keep asking questions while the crowd jeered.
Patience is the milder quality — quietly waiting things out; fortitude adds real courage, holding steady against danger, pain, or fear.
Heroism is stronger than fortitude: it goes beyond enduring hardship bravely to taking extraordinary action at great personal risk.

Endurance is the capacity to keep going through prolonged strain — the miles, the hours, the workload. It measures how long you can last. Fortitude is different: strength of mind in the face of danger, pain, or fear, whether the ordeal lasts a month or a single minute.

Grit is scrappy toughness in the long pursuit of a goal — months of setbacks, unglamorous work, getting back up again. Fortitude is not about chasing anything: it is the courage to bear what cannot be avoided. Grit chases something; fortitude withstands something.

fortuitous.definition: Fortuitous means happening by chance rather than design, often with a lucky result.
fortuitous.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fortuitous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fortuitous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A fortuitous wrong turn led the hikers straight to the waterfall they had given up on finding.
An unplanned event simply was not arranged, while a fortuitous one adds a stroke of luck to the accident.
A fortuitous encounter is a lucky accident, but a miraculous one seems to defy the odds entirely, as if chance alone could not explain it.

Accidental means happening by chance, not on purpose, and it is neutral or even negative — an accidental fire, an accidental deletion. Fortuitous keeps the accident but adds a welcome result: the wrong turn that finds the waterfall. An accidental discovery might be a disaster; a fortuitous one is a gift.

Chance, used before a noun (a chance meeting, a chance remark), simply marks something as unarranged — it takes no side on whether the outcome was good. Fortuitous usually smiles: it describes the lucky accident, the one you would never undo. Any encounter can be a chance encounter; only the welcome ones read as fortuitous.
done on purpose
brought about intentionally through planning
Sailors spoke of good fortune when the winds favored them, using the same Latin root for chance, fors, that gives fortuitous its meaning.
Fortuitous means happening by chance rather than design, often with a lucky result.
A college student left her sketchbook on a city bus.
The stranger who found it happened to be an art director at a children's publisher, and she flipped through the drawings while waiting for her stop.
Two weeks later the student, who had planned none of it, signed her first illustration contract.
The whole career began with one fortuitous mistake.
The lucky outcome came entirely from an unplanned accident, which is what fortuitous means.
neutral to formal register

fractious.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fractious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fractious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: By day three in the jury room, the twelve had grown fractious, quarreling over lunch orders as sharply as over the timeline.
Cranky is a mood one nap can fix; fractious has turned outward — snapping, digging in, making trouble for whoever's in charge.
Uncontrollable goes past fractious: nothing the handler tries works at all anymore.

Unruly means hard to control — a crowd that won't form lines, hair that won't lie flat — and it needs no bad temper at all. Fractious adds the irritability: a fractious group is hard to manage because it is snappish and quarrelsome, scraping against its handlers and itself. Unruly disobeys; fractious disobeys crossly.

Peevish is whiny and easily annoyed, usually one person at a time, sulking over small discomforts. The first violin and the violist are quarreling about bowings, the bowing quarrel is secretly about the thermostat in the van, and this morning the second violin threatened to quit over a parking space.
Their manager has begun scheduling rest days the way paramedics schedule shifts.

It isn't hatred and it isn't a feud; nobody in the van is an enemy.

fragility.definition: Fragility means the state of being easily broken or damaged, the quality of a delicate object or structure that must be handled with care.

Delicacy suggests something fine that calls for gentle handling, while fragility means the object can actually break or be damaged with very little force.

The Linden County archive holds ninety years of the town's only newspaper, and almost no one is allowed to touch it.

The paper itself will keep crumbling — nothing can stop the chemistry — but by the time it goes, every page will exist somewhere that cannot break.

fragmentary.definition: Fragmentary means made up of small disconnected pieces.
fragmentary.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fragmentary. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fragmentary should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: His memory of the crash is fragmentary - a horn, a blue fender, the smell of rain - with nothing joining the pieces.
An incomplete file is missing a page or two; fragmentary goes further down the scale of ruin - what survives is only scraps.
Patchy coverage has holes you can map; fragmentary is worse still: no stretch is whole, and the pieces barely touch.

Piecemeal describes how something arrives or gets built — one scrap at a time, over stretches of time, with no overall plan. Fragmentary judges what remains after the losses are counted: most of the whole is missing, and scraps are all that survive.

A disjointed account has all its parts on hand, but they fail to connect or flow — the telling lurches from scene to scene. Fragmentary faults survival instead: most of the whole is simply gone, and what is left cannot connect because it barely exists.

fraught.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fraught. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fraught should be able to work it out from your sentence.

Laden means weighed down with a heavy load, and the load can be anything — a ship laden with cargo, a table laden with food, a voice laden with meaning. Fraught takes only one kind of cargo: trouble. A fraught situation is loaded with tension, risk, or danger, never with anything welcome.

Charged describes an atmosphere crackling with suppressed emotion, like static before a storm — a charged silence, a charged glance. frenetic.definition: Frenetic means fast-moving and energetic in a wild, scattered, barely controlled way.
frenetic.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word frenetic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know frenetic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: By its final hour the toy drive turned frenetic — volunteers sprinting between bins, tape guns firing, and a foreman calling out numbers no one had time to write down.
Hectic is milder than frenetic — a packed, demanding stretch that still more or less follows its schedule, before the wildness sets in.
Frantic goes further than frenetic: fear or desperation takes the wheel, and the wild motion becomes a scramble to escape disaster.

Frenzied means whipped into uncontrolled excitement — the crowd, the mob, the feeding sharks. Frenetic is its everyday workplace cousin: the same wildness of motion, but usually still aimed at getting something done. A frenetic kitchen is out of breath, not out of its mind.

Breakneck is about one thing only: dangerous speed. A breakneck descent can be perfectly controlled the whole way down. Frenetic adds disorder to the speed — motion scattering in every direction as the plan loses its grip.

Historians still debate what set off the tulip frenzy of the 1630s.
Frenetic means fast-moving and energetic in a wild, scattered, barely controlled way.
When both banquets were seated at once, the hotel kitchen went frenetic: pans on every burner, three cooks colliding at the pass, and the expediter calling tickets like an auctioneer.
Frenetic is more precise than 'busy' because busyness can be orderly — a full calendar, a steady line.
Frenetic adds wildness: motion outrunning its plan, energy spraying in every direction at once.
And unlike frantic, it doesn't require fear — a kitchen can be frenetic and having the time of its life.
Frenetic is the reporter's word for energy that has outrun its plan — a frenetic trading floor, a frenetic final act.

frivolous.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word frivolous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know frivolous should be able to work it out from your sentence.

galvanize.definition: Galvanize means to shock or stir someone into sudden action.

generalize.definition: Generalize means to draw a broad conclusion from limited examples.

grievance.definition: A grievance is a wrong that someone feels justifies complaint — a real or perceived injustice, and, in formal settings, the complaint itself, stated and pursued through channels.

harangue.definition: Harangue means a long, ranting speech.
harangue.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word harangue. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know harangue should be able to work it out from your sentence.

A grumble is complaint at a mutter's volume, half meant to be overheard; it sits at the mild end, far below a harangue.

Harangue means a long, ranting speech.

harbinger.definition: Harbinger means a sign that something is coming.

A hint is the faintest rung — a trace you could miss or explain away, far milder than a harbinger.

harrowing.definition: Harrowing means deeply distressing or disturbing.
harrowing.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word harrowing. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know harrowing should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The lifeboat drill turned into a harrowing hour when the winch jammed with eight trainees swinging over open water.
Upsetting spoils an afternoon and loosens its grip by dinner — nowhere near harrowing, which drags you through an ordeal and leaves marks.
Shattering goes further than harrowing — a harrowing ordeal lets you go when it ends; a shattering loss rearranges the life that has to continue.

Harrowing means deeply distressing or disturbing.

Her grandmother read the transcript once and never touched it again.

haughty.definition: Haughty means arrogantly superior and disdainful.
haughty.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word haughty. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know haughty should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The soprano's haughty glance at the second violins said, more clearly than words, that she considered them furniture.
Proud can be quiet and deserved - pride in your work looks down on no one, while haughty always finds someone beneath it.
Contemptuous goes further than haughty: the haughty diner looks down on the waiter, while the contemptuous one sneers at him out loud.

Arrogant means claiming superiority - talking over people, assuming you deserve the first and last word - and it can be loud or entirely matter-of-fact. Haughty is one visible flavor of arrogance: cold, silent, and worn on the face, all lifted chin and withering glance.

Snobbish looks down through one narrow lens: class and taste - the right schools, the right shoes, the right accent. Haughty needs no checklist; it is a general air of icy superiority that can descend on anyone at all, whatever their standing or style.

Lofty means elevated and grand - lofty peaks, lofty ideals - and only sometimes sneers; a lofty goal can be admirable. Haughty is never a compliment: the elevation is all in the chin, and its one purpose is to place other people below it.
makes no claim to superiority
quietly declines attention or rank

Haughty comes from French haut, 'high' - still visible in haute cuisine, 'high cooking.' Because the root ends in t, adding the adjective suffix -y produces -ty and lays a perfect trap: haughty looks like an -ity noun and is neither. No everyday English word shares the root.

Haughty is pride turned outward and downward - it needs someone to look down on.
The chin lifts precisely so the eyes can descend.
Haughty is vivid and a touch literary - the word for visible, chilly superiority: the lifted chin, the withering glance.
Arrogant is the everyday workhorse; snobbish targets class and taste.

hedonist.definition: Hedonist means one who believes pleasure should be the primary pursuit of humans.
hedonist.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word hedonist. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know hedonist should be able to work it out from your sentence.

A fun-lover is milder than a hedonist: happy to take pleasure when it arrives, never reorganizing life around it.
A bon vivant savors good living — fine tables, good company — but stops short of the hedonist's full creed that pleasure is the point of everything.

A pleasure-seeker is anyone out chasing enjoyment — a single indulgent weekend earns the plain compound. A hedonist is a pleasure-seeker with a philosophy: pleasure is not one pursuit among many but the measure every choice must answer to. The seeking can be casual; the hedonism is a creed.

A sybarite is devoted to luxury — silk, spas, long baths, fine rooms — pleasure pursued through expense and comfort. A hedonist needs no money at all: the creed is only that pleasure, cheap or costly, is the point of a life. Sybarite names the taste; hedonist names the philosophy.

Hedonist means one who believes pleasure should be the primary pursuit of humans.

Her sister calls it laziness.

hegemony.definition: Hegemony means the controlling dominance of one power over the rest.
hegemony.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word hegemony. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know hegemony should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Nobody voted for English's hegemony over the sciences; laboratories in forty countries simply stopped publishing in anything else.
Leverage is far short of hegemony — strength for one negotiation, a good hand in a single game, spent when the deal closes; hegemony is a standing position the whole field steers by.
Empire goes further than hegemony — the hegemon's rivals keep their own flags and follow its lead; an empire hauls the flags down and rules directly.

Dominance is the plain word for being on top, and it can be won one contest at a time — a team can dominate a season and be gone the next. Hegemony adds the standing arrangement: the others steer by the leader's lead and reshape their own plans around it.

Supremacy is the title for holding top rank — a claim about position, the name engraved on the trophy. Hegemony is the working arrangement underneath: one power setting terms that its supposed equals follow. Supremacy can be asserted in a slogan; hegemony shows up in everyone else's behavior.
a contest still undecided — nobody yet sets the terms

Greek hegemon, the leader, produced hegemony and its adjective hegemonic — and then stopped. No everyday English word shares the root, so anchor the meaning to the picture instead: one flag out front, and the rest of the fleet steering by it.

heinous.definition: Heinous means shockingly wicked — describing an act or crime so evil that it provokes outrage.
heinous.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word heinous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know heinous should be able to work it out from your sentence.

Calling an act wrong notes a moral failure, but calling it heinous means it is so evil that it shocks people.

hereditary.definition: Hereditary means passed down genetically from parent to offspring.
hereditary.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word hereditary. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know hereditary should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The breeder traced the hereditary coat pattern through six generations of her herd.
Familial says only that a trait runs in a family, which could be diet or habit as easily as descent, while hereditary says it travels in the genes.
Genetic is the most precise of the three, since every hereditary trait is genetic, but a genetic change arising new in one individual is not hereditary until it is passed on.

Inherited is the everyday word for anything received from those who came before, from a grandmother's ring to a gene for eye colour. Hereditary is the formal adjective for what descent itself transmits, and in medicine it points specifically to transmission through the parents' genes.

Ancestral ties something to one's forebears -- ancestral land, an ancestral custom -- without saying how it travelled down. Hereditary names the mechanism: passed from parent to offspring, in medicine through the genes. A recipe can be ancestral; a blood type is hereditary.

Hereditary means passed down genetically from parent to offspring.
A vet compiles records on 240 collies living in one valley.

Two litters raised in different counties turn up the same defect in the same proportion.
The vet concludes that the condition is hereditary.

The defect follows one sire's bloodline rather than the shared pasture, water, or feed, and reappears in pups raised elsewhere, which marks a trait travelling by descent, exactly what hereditary means.
technical in biology and law; neutral
Hereditary covers anything transmitted by descent, whether a gene, a title, or a monarchy.

In medicine it is the narrower cousin of congenital, taught in this unit: congenital means only that a condition was present at birth, while hereditary specifies that it arrived through the parents' genes.

Hereditary is the formal adjective for what descent itself transmits, and in medicine it points specifically to transmission through the parents' genes.

In 1853 Queen Victoria's youngest son, Leopold, bled alarmingly from small scrapes, and the palace doctors could neither explain it nor stop it.
The disorder, haemophilia, was hereditary: it travelled through the family's genes, passed from mother to son in a pattern no physician of the day could yet read.
Victoria's daughters showed no symptoms themselves, yet several of their sons developed the same fragile blood.
Nothing about palace life caused it.
Royal cousins raised in different countries, on different diets, under different doctors, bled the same way.
The trait was not a habit of the household but a fact of descent, written into the line itself.

hesitant.definition: Hesitant means slow to act because of uncertainty.
hesitant.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word hesitant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know hesitant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The new lifeguard was hesitant on his first whistle, unsure whether the swimmers were really too far out.
Unsure is the milder state — you can be unsure and still act quickly; hesitant means the uncertainty is visibly slowing you down.
Paralyzed is far stronger than hesitant: a paralyzed decision-maker cannot act at all, while a hesitant one acts late and haltingly.

Reluctant means unwilling — you drag your feet because you do not want to do the thing at all. Hesitant is about doubt, not desire: a hesitant person usually wants to act and is slowed by uncertainty. A reluctant witness resents being called at all; a hesitant one wants to speak but keeps stalling.

Tentative describes the cautious, unconfident manner of an action, or a plan made only provisionally — a tentative knock, a tentative agreement. Hesitant is about the delay itself: uncertainty slowing you down before you act at all. A tentative step is soft and careful; a hesitant one is late in coming.
sure of oneself
keen to act at once
The nurse peeled the backing off the adhesive and laid the bandage flat against his arm.
Hesitant means slow to act because of uncertainty.
The scholarship application sat open on Jun's laptop for eleven days.
He reread the essay prompt each night, typed a sentence, and deleted it.
His teachers had told him he was exactly the kind of candidate the program wanted, but he kept wondering if his grades from freshman year would sink him.
The night before the deadline, the form was still blank.
Jun wasn't lazy or uninterested — he was hesitant, and his uncertainty had nearly cost him the chance.
Jun's slowness to act — eleven days of typing and deleting — flows directly from his uncertainty about his own chances, which is exactly what hesitant means.
Hesitant is the adjective for a person or manner ('a hesitant knock'); its verb cousin hesitate names the pause itself.
Being hesitant is about uncertainty, not refusal — a hesitant person usually wants to act and can't quite start.

The spring musical's auditions ran long, and by four o'clock only two names remained on the sign-up sheet.
Devon wanted the lead badly — he had rehearsed the audition song for weeks and told his friends as much.

Yet when his name was called he stood hesitant in the wings, smoothing the sheet music, stepping toward the stage and back twice, wondering whether his voice had fully recovered from last week's cold.
The director finally waved him forward, and once he began, he sang without a single crack.
Afterward Devon joked that the hardest part of the whole audition had been the six feet between the curtain and the piano.

heterodox.definition: Heterodox means contrary to accepted or established belief.
heterodox.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word heterodox. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know heterodox should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her heterodox training plan — rest days before races, no morning runs — contradicted nearly everything the coaching manuals prescribed.
Questioning merely asks whether the accepted view holds; it stops well short of heterodox.
Dissenting goes further than questioning — it openly disagrees — but usually with one decision; heterodox sets a whole position against the established doctrine itself.

Nonconforming means declining to follow the group's practices — dress, ritual, procedure — in behavior as much as in belief. Heterodox is narrower and aims at doctrine: a heterodox position sets its claims against the established teaching itself. You can be nonconforming in what you wear; you are heterodox only in what you believe.

Unorthodox says a method or choice departs from standard practice — an unorthodox batting stance, an unorthodox route to a degree. Heterodox is the heavier, doctrinal cousin: it stands against a settled body of accepted belief, so there must be an orthodoxy to defy. A technique can be unorthodox; a theology or a theory is heterodox.
matching what most people already accept
no longer in dispute; agreed by nearly everyone
Zeno's most famous paradox still opens the first lecture of the philosophy survey.
Heterodox means contrary to accepted or established belief.
The conservatory's youngest piano instructor holds a heterodox view of practice: scales, she argues, should come last, after a student can already play songs by ear.
The senior faculty invited her to defend the idea at a colloquium mostly, one admitted, in hopes of talking her out of it — every method book on the shelf teaches the reverse.

Heterodox is more precise than 'unconventional' because it points at belief: it means contrary to accepted or established doctrine, so there has to be an orthodoxy — a settled teaching — for a position to stand against.
A strange haircut is unconventional; a theory the whole field rejects is heterodox.
Heterodox lives in academic and religious argument, where a settled doctrine exists to stand against; it describes positions and thinkers, not haircuts.
In this unit, keep it apart from its neighbors: a maverick defies the group in conduct, an iconoclast attacks its institutions, but heterodox describes the belief itself.
