For his final broadcast, the station gave its retiring weatherman ninety seconds to say goodbye.

He used them to forecast the station's future: 'Cloudy, with a strong chance of reruns, and viewers advised to seek shelter from the nine o'clock lineup.' The control room laughed so hard the credits rolled late — and the program director's smile, colleagues noted, never reached his eyes.
Critics called the send-off mordant: every line got its laugh, and every laugh left a tooth mark somewhere in the building.
The station aired it too, having apparently decided that being bitten in public was better than being ignored.

mores.definition: Mores means the fixed customs and moral attitudes of a group.
mores.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word mores. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know mores should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Nothing in the dorm handbook covers it, but hall mores are strict: you do not run the blender during quiet hours, and you replace what you borrow.
Customs are the milder rung — what people usually do, like cake on birthdays; skipping a custom makes you odd, while breaking mores marks a failure of decency.
Laws go further than mores: a law is written down and enforced by courts, while mores are enforced only by a community's regard — though losing that can hurt worse than a fine.

Folkways are the small everyday habits of a people — greetings, table rhythms, which nights the market runs — and they are lightly held. Mores carry moral charge: neglecting a folkway makes you unusual, while breaking mores makes the town doubt your decency.

Norms are all of a group's shared expectations, from dress codes to how a line forms, whatever their weight. Mores are the narrower, heavier set — the norms a community treats as matters of right and wrong, enforced by moral judgment rather than raised eyebrows.
no shared expectations holding at all
conduct with no common code behind it
Her lecture on the poem took a sudden moral turn in its last ten minutes.
Mores means the fixed customs and moral attitudes of a group.

In the county where my father grew up, mores govern a funeral more firmly than any statute: neighbors mow the family's lawn without asking, casseroles arrive unsigned, and nobody sells the bereaved anything for a month.
No council passed these rules and no court could enforce them.
Breaking one simply tells the town, permanently, what you are.
Mores is the precise term because these are the fixed customs and moral attitudes of a group — heavier than manners, which merely smooth social traffic.
Skipping the casserole is not impolite; it is felt as a small failure of decency.
That moral charge, enforced by regard rather than law, is what the word names.
Mores is the sociologist's word — always plural, pronounced MOR-ayz — for the customs a group treats as matters of decency.
Etiquette governs forks; mores govern what neighbors owe each other.

Within this unit, keep the lanes: mores are what a community's conscience requires, ritualized describes the fixed form a practice has hardened into, and quotidian describes the everyday texture of what recurs.

Aboard a nineteenth-century whaling ship, almost nothing was written down, yet the crew's mores governed the voyage more tightly than the owner's contract did.
A sailor who shirked a watch was mocked; that was a lapse of habit.
But a sailor who stole from a shipmate's sea chest had done something worse in the crew's eyes.
Thieves were not merely teased.
Men refused to eat beside them, and at the next port they often found no ship willing to sign them on.
Historians note that no law required any of this.
The punishment ran on shared moral judgment, passed from forecastle to forecastle.
The code answered a real need: months at sea left no room for a man the others could not trust.

morose.definition: Morose means sunk in gloom that has settled in and pushes company away.
morose.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word morose. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know morose should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: After the bakery turned down his sourdough, Amos was morose for a week, kneading in silence and glaring at the proofing loaves.
Glum is milder than morose — a passing afternoon of low spirits, while a morose mood sinks into gloom that settles in and turns sullen enough to push company away.
Despairing goes further than morose — beyond gloom into the conviction that nothing will ever improve.

Sullen is silent resentment: the slammed door, the one-word answers aimed at whoever caused the mood. Morose shares the gloom but drops the grudge — a morose person is sunk in darkness that has settled in for weeks, not punishing anyone in particular.

Melancholy means gently, thoughtfully sad — wistful autumn evenings, old letters, a mood a person can almost enjoy. Morose strips away that sweetness: the gloom turns heavy and unsociable, with a sullen edge that pushes company away rather than inviting quiet reflection.
heartily, laughingly good-humored
briskly cheerful and energetic
One daring rescue at sea lifted the whole fleet's morale for a month.
Morose means sunk in gloom that has settled in and pushes company away.
Nobody could tease the old ferryman out of his morose spells: whole crossings passed in sighs and one-word answers, the passengers' jokes sinking into the grey water behind the boat.
Morose is deeper than a bad mood: settled gloom with an unsociable edge that pushes company away.
A glum person is quiet for an afternoon; a morose one has let the darkness move in and answer the door.
Morose is settled gloom that pushes company away — days or weeks of it, not a passing cloud.
'Glum' covers an afternoon; morose moves in and unpacks.
And where its unit-mate dour describes only the stern, unsmiling surface, morose reports the weather inside: genuinely dark.
A dour face can hide contentment; a morose one never does.

When Uncle Rodrigo sold the restaurant, everyone expected a few quiet weeks.
The gloom arrived in June and simply stayed: curtains half drawn, calls unreturned, the chessboard on the porch untouched.
He wasn't angry with the buyers, and he said so; he wasn't angry with anyone.
The darkness had no address.
By September, neighbors who dropped off soup had stopped ringing the bell.
He would wave them off from the window, not unkindly, and go back to his chair.
It was his sister who finally named the difference: sadness visits, she said, but this had moved in — heavy, unsocial, and in no hurry to leave.

motif.definition: Motif means a distinctive element — an image, phrase, or design — that repeats throughout a work of art, literature, or music, gaining force with each return.
motif.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word motif. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know motif should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Interlocking waves ripple across the hotel's carpets, curtains, and tilework — a motif the designer carried into every room.
An echo is fainter than a motif: an image may echo once or twice across a work, while a motif returns so often that the repetition itself begins to carry meaning.
A leitmotif goes further than a motif: a motif recurs freely, but a leitmotif is bound by design to one character or idea and sounds every time that presence enters.

Theme means the idea a work keeps exploring, stated in the abstract — loyalty, decay, forgiveness. A theme is an idea; a motif is the concrete image, phrase, or figure that keeps returning to carry it.

Refrain means the repeated line of a song or poem, coming back word for word in its fixed place. A motif returns too, but freely — in new forms, new keys, new corners of the work — rather than as an exact repeat.

Symbol means an image or object that stands for a larger idea — and it can do that in a single appearance. A motif earns its force by returning again and again, whether or not it stands for anything at all.
a one-off that breaks the pattern instead of making one
something appearing for the very first time — its point is that it has never come before
A restored locomotive draws photographers to the valley every October.
Motif means a distinctive element — an image, phrase, or design — that repeats throughout a work of art, literature, or music, gaining force with each return.

Halfway through the songwriting workshop, Elena noticed that a three-note falling figure kept surfacing in her ballad — under the first verse, beneath the bridge, and again, slowed to half speed, in the final chorus.
She stopped fighting the motif and made it the song's signature.
One small musical figure, returning in verse, bridge, and chorus until the repetition itself stitches the song together — a recurring element like that is exactly what a motif is.
neutral — the critic's and designer's word
Motif belongs to the vocabulary of analysis: reviewers, art historians, and English teachers reach for it when a work repeats itself on purpose.
It applies as easily to wallpaper as to literature — a paisley motif, a betrayal motif.
Keep it apart from theme (the abstract idea) and from symbol (the stand-in): a motif need not mean anything at all; it need only return.
Watch the sound-alike motto, which is a saying to live by, not a repeating element.

Assembling the painter Iris Chen's fifty-year retrospective, curator Malik Rowe hung the canvases in order and noticed what reviewers had missed.
A red kite appears in her earliest student work, small and far away.
It returns in the harbor scenes of her middle years, tangled in rigging, and again in the late desert paintings, reduced to a diamond of color on the horizon.
Rowe stopped calling it a coincidence and began calling it a motif: the kite changes size, setting, and even shape, but it keeps coming back, and each return gathers up the ones before.
In the catalog he wrote that by the final room the kite no longer needs the sky — a red diamond on a kitchen table is enough to make visitors think of flight.
Chen, asked about it at the opening, only smiled and said that some images refuse to be finished with a painter.

mountainous.definition: Mountainous means having many mountains, or relating to high, rugged terrain.
mountainous.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word mountainous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know mountainous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Three quarters of the country is mountainous, and only the coastal strip is flat enough to farm.
Hilly ground rises and falls but never reaches true peaks, while mountainous country does.
Alpine is narrower than mountainous, pointing at the high, treeless zone near the summits rather than at the whole mountain landscape.

Rugged means rough, steep, and hard to cross -- a word about texture and difficulty, not height, so a rugged coastline can lie at sea level. Mountainous is the height claim: country that rises into true mountains, whether the going is rough or gentle.

Craggy describes rock that is steep, broken, and jagged, and a craggy headland can stand at the edge of the sea. Mountainous speaks to the scale of whole country -- land built up into real mountains -- rather than to the texture of its rock.
without significant variation in height
lying low, near sea level
The negotiators agreed that the hostages' safety was paramount and let every other demand wait.
Mountainous means having many mountains, or relating to high, rugged terrain.
A rail company costs two routes of equal length between the same two cities.
The northern route crosses flat farmland and needs nine bridges, no tunnels, and a maximum gradient of one percent.
The southern route climbs three passes above 2,000 metres, requires fourteen tunnels and thirty-one viaducts, and closes for snow most winters.
The engineers price the southern line at four times the northern one, because the country it crosses is mountainous.
Three passes above 2,000 metres, fourteen tunnels, and regular winter closures describe country built of high peaks rather than gentle ground, which is what mountainous means.
Mountainous describes the land itself and, by extension, anything of mountain size, as in a mountainous pile of laundry.
It names one kind of terrain rather than the general subject of terrain, since the arrangement of a region's surface features as a whole is its topography, taught elsewhere in this unit.

The land between is relentlessly mountainous: ridge after ridge above four thousand metres, with glaciers filling the high valleys.
The road they finally built swings two hundred kilometres out of its way to follow a single river gorge through the ranges.
Even so, it crosses three passes, and each winter the highest of them closes under six metres of snow.
Flat ground is so scarce along the way that the only petrol station for a day's drive stands on land blasted level from the slope.

multifaceted.definition: Multifaceted means having many different sides or aspects.
multifaceted.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word multifaceted. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know multifaceted should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Restoring the old mill proved multifaceted work — part carpentry, part hydrology, part fundraising, and part town politics.
Two-sided grants exactly two aspects — every argument has that much — and stops far short of multifaceted.
Layered goes further than two-sided, stacking level on level, but it stops short of multifaceted, which opens onto many distinct sides at once.

Many-sided is the everyday phrasing for a thing with several aspects, and it stops at counting them. Multifaceted adds the gem's discipline: the many sides all belong to one object, distinct faces of a single whole. Many-sided notes the number; multifaceted keeps the sides attached to one thing.

Complex means made of interwoven parts that resist quick understanding — the difficulty lives in the tangling. Multifaceted only says one thing shows many distinct sides; those sides may each be simple. A multifaceted job can be four easy tasks; a complex problem knots its parts together.
showing a single aspect and nothing more
plain and easily taken in at a glance
Scaffolding hid the theater's facade for most of the spring.
Multifaceted means having many different sides or aspects.

Ask the park's head ranger what her job is and she will hand you Tuesday's log: a sunrise search for two lost hikers, a mid-morning grant report, an afternoon spent re-routing a trail around a goshawk nest, and an evening lecture on bears.
One position, and a multifaceted one — four professions folded into a single badge.

Multifaceted is more precise than 'varied' because it keeps everything attached to one thing: a facet is one polished face of a single gem, so a multifaceted job, mind, or problem is one object turning many distinct sides toward you.
If the pieces do not belong to a whole, they are simply many — call them manifold instead.
Multifaceted is the boardroom-and-classroom word for one thing with many sides — a role, a crisis, a personality.
Keep the gem in mind to separate it from its unit-mates: multifaceted is one stone with many faces, manifold is many varied things, and complex adds that the parts tangle.
If you only mean 'complicated,' say that.

Multifaceted adds the gem's discipline: the many sides all belong to one object, distinct faces of a single whole.
Many-sided notes the number; multifaceted keeps the sides attached to one thing.

When Maple Falls hired a coordinator for its centennial, the council admitted up front that the position was multifaceted.
One week she was in the archives, checking dates for the history pageant; the next she was pricing tents and folding tables for the fairgrounds.
She scheduled the parade, recruited food vendors, and set up a booth where residents recorded memories of the old cannery.
None of the tasks was difficult on its own, and she often finished two in a morning.
What made the job remarkable was that permits, pageants, and oral histories were all sides of a single celebration, and she had to keep every side turning at once.

multifarious.definition: Multifarious means of many different kinds; highly varied.
multifarious.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word multifarious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know multifarious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Grandpa's multifarious toolbox held watch screwdrivers, fishing lures, sheet music, and a folding dentist's mirror.
Varied stops short of multifarious — a varied program has options, while a multifarious one seems to contain everything.
Kaleidoscopic goes further than multifarious — the variety is not just wide but shifting dazzlingly before your eyes.

Diverse says the members of a group genuinely differ from one another — a diverse committee, diverse habitats. Multifarious pushes the same idea toward astonishment: not just real differences, but so many different kinds at once that the sheer spread of the collection surprises you.

Assorted describes a modest mix of kinds gathered in one place — assorted chocolates, assorted screws in a jar. Multifarious operates at a grander scale: many genuinely different kinds at once, a range wide enough to startle. A drawer is assorted; a century-old general store is multifarious.
all exactly the same
holding to one kind without change

Multi- is everywhere in English — multiple, multitude, multiplex — but the word's other half, Latin -fariam ('in so many parts or ways'), survives in no other common word. Let the familiar multi- remind you of the meaning, and learn multifarious as its own word.
Multifarious means of many different kinds; highly varied.

The general store survived a century by stocking multifarious goods: snowshoes hung above canning jars, violin strings shared a drawer with fuse wire, and the storekeeper could produce a wedding veil or a wolf trap with equal speed.
Multifarious insists on more than number—'numerous' merely counts the items, while multifarious says the items are of genuinely different kinds, a range wide enough to surprise.

myopic.definition: Myopic means lacking foresight; focused only on the short term.

nomadic.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word nomadic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know nomadic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The young male wolf led a nomadic life for two years, crossing four mountain ranges without ever holding a territory.
Mobile means only that something is able to move, while nomadic says the moving never stops long enough to make a permanent home.
Itinerant is nomadic's close cousin, but it usually describes people travelling for work, such as an itinerant repairman, rather than a whole way of life.

Wandering means moving about with no fixed home or destination, and it can describe one lost afternoon as easily as a lifetime. Nomadic makes the larger claim: the wandering is the whole way of life, permanent and organized around movement.

Drifting means moving along with no aim at all, carried wherever chance takes you. Nomadic life also lacks a fixed home, but its movement has purpose -- herders track pasture, crossbill flocks track cone crops -- so a nomadic people is not simply drifting.
living permanently in one place
staying in one place rather than moving
Historians use nomadism for the whole way of life a nomadic people follows, and it is very nearly the only common English relative this root ever produced.
Nomadic means wandering from place to place rather than settling permanently.
Most songbirds of the boreal forest keep to the same few hectares all their lives.
A flock ringed in Finland one autumn turned up 1,400 kilometres east the next year, then in Norway the year after, always where the spruce cones hung heaviest and never twice in the same wood.
Because cone crops fail unpredictably, the birds can hold neither a fixed route nor a fixed home, and their nomadic habit is the only way they keep eating.
Birds that travel 1,400 kilometres to wherever the cones are heaviest, never return to the same wood, and hold no home range at all are wandering rather than settling, which is the heart of nomadic.

Nomadic describes a pattern of living rather than wildness or automatic behaviour, so keep it clear of feral (a domesticated animal now living wild) and instinctive (a single automatic behaviour) elsewhere in this unit.
Note too that nomadic movement is unpredictable and homeless by definition, which is what separates it from a seasonal journey along a fixed route.

Families followed the grazing with their camel herds, and twice a year great salt caravans crossed the desert to trade.
Their nomadic life was not aimless roaming.
Every route was set by wells that could not be missed and by pastures that lasted only a few weeks.
Households carried their architecture with them: tents of hide and woven mats that two people could raise in an hour.
To settle in one place, the elders said, was to watch your herds strip the land bare around you; the desert fed only those who kept moving.

nonchalant.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word nonchalant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know nonchalant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The bomb-disposal veteran talked about defusing mines in the same nonchalant tone most people use for grocery lists.
Relaxed just means at ease; nonchalant goes further, wearing visible unconcern about something most people would react to.
Blasé outdoes nonchalant: the nonchalant winner may be hiding a racing heart, while the blasé one has genuinely stopped being impressed by winning at all.

Unruffled means the calm is real: something disruptive happened and it genuinely failed to disturb you. The word reports your true state, not a look. Nonchalant reports only the appearance of unconcern — a nonchalant shrug can hide a racing pulse, where an unruffled person truly is not rattled.

Unfazed means not actually thrown off by something startling or difficult — the composure is genuine, and the word vouches for it. Nonchalant makes no such promise: it names the cool, unconcerned surface a person shows, which may be a careful act covering plenty of worry underneath.
visibly rattled and disorganized
twitchy with nerves
The label says one granola bar packs two hundred calories of energy.
Nonchalant means appearing calmly unconcerned.
The valedictorian found out mid-shift at the diner.
Her manager read the email aloud over the milkshake machine; she nodded, said 'cool,' and went back to wiping the counter — utterly nonchalant.
Only her sister, watching from a corner booth, saw her squeeze the rag until her knuckles whitened.
Nonchalant is the exact word because it describes the appearance of unconcern, true or not: the whitened knuckles tell us the calm is a performance.
Indifferent would claim she genuinely did not care — a very different, and here plainly false, report.
Nonchalant reports only the surface: calm unconcern on display, whatever churns beneath.
That makes it the word for cool performances — and different from its cluster-mates indifferent (the concern truly absent) and apathetic (the capacity to care gone).
Casually is its adverb cousin: a nonchalant shrug is given casually.

The cast braced for panic.
Instead Priya kept eating her noodles and asked, between bites, whether the follow-spot operator knew about the change.
All evening her castmates marveled at the nonchalant way she handled it — a shrug at the wig fitting, a joke in the wings.
Only her roommate knew about the twenty minutes after the show, when Priya sat in the parking lot gripping the steering wheel until her hands stopped shaking.
The unconcern, in other words, had been a costume too — worn perfectly, and taken off only when no one was watching.

normative.definition: Normative means relating to an ideal standard, model, or rule of behavior that things are expected to conform to.
normative.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word normative. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know normative should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The ethics committee's report made a normative argument about how researchers should treat their volunteers.
Customary is weaker than normative: a customary practice is just what people usually do, while a normative rule says what they ought to do.
Compulsory is stronger than normative: a normative standard tells you what you should do, but a compulsory rule forces you to comply.

Prescriptive means laying down rules for how things should be done — a prescriptive grammar tells you which usages to avoid. Normative is one notch more abstract: relating to standards of how things ought to be, even when no rule is issued. A claim can be normative without prescribing anything; prescriptive language always issues the rule.

Standard-setting describes whatever establishes the model others are expected to follow — a standard-setting body, a standard-setting performance. Normative describes anything concerned with such standards: claims, theories, and assumptions about how things ought to be. A standard-setting act creates the benchmark; a normative claim appeals to one.
describing how things actually are, without judging how they should be
The enormous pumpkin at the fair needed four volunteers and a hand truck just to reach the weighing platform.
Normative means relating to an ideal standard, model, or rule of behavior that things are expected to conform to.

In her philosophy seminar, Jalen's professor wrote two sentences on the board: 'Most drivers exceed the speed limit' and 'Drivers should obey the speed limit.' She explained that the first sentence merely reports a fact about the world, while the second is a normative claim, because it appeals to a standard of how people ought to behave.
For the rest of the semester, students practiced spotting the moment an argument quietly slid from facts into normative territory.
The second sentence expresses a standard of how people should act rather than reporting how they do act, which is exactly what makes it normative.
academic register (ethics, social science, linguistics)

The first was a survey: how many people cross the bridge each day, where the noise is worst, which lots have stood empty for a decade.
The second made a normative argument — that the district ought to put housing before parking, and that a waterfront belongs to those who walk it, not to those who drive past.
At the hearing, the difference mattered.
Nobody disputed the bridge counts, but the second document drew a line of speakers, some praising its vision, others calling its ideals someone else's.
As one commissioner put it, the survey told the city what the district is; the argument told the city what it should be.

novice.definition: Novice means a beginner without training or experience.
novice.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word novice. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know novice should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The forge master starts each novice on nails — a thousand of them, until the hammer stops bouncing.
A rookie has less learning ahead than a novice — the rookie's training is finished and the job is held, with only a first season left to prove, while the novice is still on day one of instruction.
A raw recruit goes further than a novice — the novice has begun learning the ropes; the recruit reports on day one having never seen them.

Beginner is the plain, all-purpose word for someone just starting out — any activity, any setting, no story attached. A novice is a beginner seen from inside a discipline: unproven, supervised, learning the ropes under instruction. Every novice is a beginner; beginner alone claims nothing about training.

A trainee is a beginner already enrolled in a formal program, answering to an instructor and a syllabus. A novice may be just as green with no program anywhere — the word marks the inexperience itself, not the enrollment. Every trainee begins as a novice; not every novice signs up.
the craft fully owned
the years and the scars already banked

Novice means a beginner without training or experience.

Nobody expected him to: the academy takes true novices on purpose, teaching its own methods to hands that have nothing to unlearn, and by October he could rig a hose lay blindfolded.
Novice is the exact word because a novice is a beginner without training or experience — the blank slate itself.
The word doesn't predict failure; it marks a starting line.
Monasteries used it first for the untested newcomer under instruction, and the sense has never wandered: supervised, unproven, day one.
Novice is the standard, unfussy word for a beginner, at home on official forms — novice class, novice division.
Its twin in this unit, neophyte, says the same thing in Greek dress and suits magazine prose.
If the beginner's mistakes rather than status are the point, greenhorn; if it's the first year on a real job, rookie.

Mara had no certificate program behind her and none ahead; the studio taught the old way, one unproven pair of hands under one master's eye.
Her first weeks were a record of small failures — cracked punties, lopsided cups — each one examined with her teacher before the shards went in the bin.

noxious.definition: Noxious means harmful or poisonous, especially to breathe or be exposed to.
noxious.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word noxious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know noxious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Never mix bleach with ammonia: the pair releases noxious fumes that can sear your lungs in seconds.
An unpleasant smell merely offends the nose, while a noxious one can genuinely harm you.
A lethal gas is the extreme beyond noxious — deadly outright, not just harmful.

Toxic means poisonous to the body, and it is a property a substance carries wherever it sits — in a bottle, a bloodstream, or a landfill. Noxious adds the idea of exposure: fumes, gases, and vapors that harm people who breathe or contact them. Sealed mercury is toxic; the vapor escaping a broken seal is noxious.

Poisonous means capable of causing illness or death, and the harm usually travels by swallowing or touch — poisonous berries, a poisonous bite. Noxious harm arrives mostly on the air: fumes and gases that hurt you simply through exposure. A berry is poisonous on the tongue; a gas leak is noxious in the lungs.
causing no damage at all
clean and safe to breathe
After eight years, new evidence proved the night janitor innocent.
Noxious means harmful or poisonous, especially to breathe or be exposed to.
On the first day of chemistry lab, Mr.
Okafor pointed to the glass-fronted cabinet along the wall.

An air-quality team traced the problem to idling work trains staged overnight in the dead-end tunnel, where exhaust pooled instead of venting to the street.

Carbon monoxide and diesel particulates sat at levels the state classifies as noxious — air that injures the people who breathe it, not air that is merely stale.

nuance.definition: Nuance means a slight variation in meaning, tone, or expression.
nuance.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word nuance. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know nuance should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Chat strips the nuance out of a joke; the wink that saves it in person doesn't survive as a semicolon and a parenthesis.
A distinction goes further than a nuance — it's a difference you can state in one plain sentence, where a nuance is felt before it can be named.
A gulf goes further than a distinction, and much further than a nuance — the difference grown so wide it separates: two positions that no longer share a category, let alone a shade.

A shade is the smallest difference of all — the gap between two blues, borrowed for meanings: a shade of doubt, a shade warmer. It is a nuance wearing its color metaphor, a variation almost too small to state. Nuance is the general word for the same fine difference in tone or meaning.

Subtlety is the fineness itself — of a flavor, a design, an argument — praising how delicately a thing is done, at any scale. A nuance is one particular small difference in meaning, tone, or expression. You admire a translator's subtlety in general; you point at the exact nuance she kept.
differences mashed flat
the version painted too wide to be exact
Latin nubes, 'cloud,' drifted into French as nue and stopped there — no other everyday English word kept the root, so nuance stands alone, trailing its clouds.

None of it could be caught in a lyric sheet.
Fans who printed both versions side by side found the pages identical.

nullified.definition: Nullified means made officially void; deprived of legal force.
nullified.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word nullified. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know nullified should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The waiver Marcus signed at the trampoline park was nullified the day a judge confirmed he had been fifteen when he signed it.
Challenged is milder than nullified — a challenged ruling wobbles but still binds until someone with authority acts, while a nullified one has already lost its force.
Erased goes a step beyond nullified: a nullified ruling still sits in the file, stripped of force, while an erased one vanishes from the record entirely.

Voided is the plain, everyday legal stamp: no-longer-counts. Nullified means the same deadness with a more formal, weightier ring — a court nullifies a patent; a cashier voids a receipt. Reach for nullified when real legal force is at stake, voided for routine paperwork.

Overturned means reversed by a higher authority on review — and usually something new stands in the old ruling's place. Nullified merely switches the legal force off: nothing need replace the dead ruling, which often simply stops counting from the moment it was signed.
confirmed as valid and still binding
given effect — made to actually happen

Nullified means made officially void; deprived of legal force.

Nullified is force switched off: the paper survives, the signatures remain, but in law the thing no longer counts.
Rulings, contracts, patents, results — anything whose power comes from law can be nullified.
Say nullified when something's legal force has been switched off — a ruling, patent, waiver, or result that no longer counts.
Annul (this unit) is the act of erasing a thing as if it never was; abrogate (this unit) is authority killing a law or pact.
Nullified reports the resulting deadness.

nurture.definition: Nurture means to care for something and help it develop.
nurture.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word nurture. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know nurture should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Bakers nurture a sourdough starter for years, feeding it by the clock and guarding it from drafts.
Tend is milder than nurture — tending covers the basic chores, water the plant, feed the cat, with no promise of anything more, while nurture aims every feeding at growth.
Coddle goes further than nurture — nurture builds strength toward independence, while coddling protects so completely that nothing ever toughens.

Raise means to bring up a child or an animal until it is grown — the word is tied to that job and ends when the growing-up does. Nurture travels wider and needs no finish line: you can nurture a talent, a friendship, or a project, adjusting the care daily so it develops.

To look after something is to keep it safe and fed — the sitter looks after the dog, and success is nothing going wrong. Nurture aims past looking after: nurture points the same care at growth, at helping the thing become more than it was.

obdurate.definition: Obdurate means unyielding to persuasion, pity, or moral appeals.
obdurate.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word obdurate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know obdurate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The warden stayed obdurate even after hundreds of letters begged him to reopen the old case.
Firm describes someone who holds a position steadily but can still be reasoned with; obdurate goes further, suggesting a heart hardened against every plea.
Implacable is even stronger than obdurate — an implacable person cannot be appeased at all, ever, while an obdurate one is 'merely' deaf to persuasion and pity.

Unyielding means refusing to give ground under any kind of pressure — force, argument, demands, time. Obdurate is narrower and darker: hardened specifically against appeals to pity, conscience, and persuasion. A cliff face is unyielding; only a heart that hears the plea and still refuses is obdurate.

Hardhearted names a general lack of pity or warmth toward others' suffering — an everyday word for a cold nature. Obdurate is more specific and more literary: appeals have actually been made — tears, arguments, conscience — and every one has bounced off. A hardhearted person may never be tested; an obdurate one refuses appeal after appeal.
softening and giving in
easily moved to sympathy
The stone bridge has endured two centuries of spring floods without losing a single arch.
Obdurate means unyielding to persuasion, pity, or moral appeals.
For ten years, descendants of the sculptor asked the collector to return the bronze figure to their village square.
Historians wrote open letters, and schoolchildren mailed drawings of the empty pedestal.
The collector read every appeal, admitted the family's grief was real, and refused each request without exception.
Friends said no appeal to conscience had ever moved him on any matter of property.
His heart, one curator sighed, was simply obdurate.
The collector hears every emotional and moral appeal, admits they are moving, and still refuses every single time — that hardened resistance to pity is exactly what obdurate describes.
formal, literary; usually disapproving
Obdurate is the harshest of this unit's 'stubborn' words: it suggests a heart hardened against pity or moral appeals specifically.
Unlike obstinate (a general refusal to change one's mind or course) or adamant (loud, emphatic insistence on a particular point), obdurate implies that even tears and conscience cannot get through.
unyielding: Unyielding means refusing to give ground under any kind of pressure — force, argument, demands, time.
Obdurate is narrower and darker: hardened specifically against appeals to pity, conscience, and persuasion.
A cliff face is unyielding; only a heart that hears the plea and still refuses is obdurate.
hardhearted: Hardhearted names a general lack of pity or warmth toward others' suffering — an everyday word for a cold nature.
Obdurate is more specific and more literary: appeals have actually been made — tears, arguments, conscience — and every one has bounced off.
A hardhearted person may never be tested; an obdurate one refuses appeal after appeal.
relenting: softening and giving in
softhearted: easily moved to sympathy
firm → obdurate → implacable
obdurate: Firm describes someone who holds a position steadily but can still be reasoned with; obdurate goes further, suggesting a heart hardened against every plea.
obdurate: Implacable is even stronger than obdurate — an implacable person cannot be appeased at all, ever, while an obdurate one is 'merely' deaf to persuasion and pity.
When the reservoir company announced it would flood the valley, the village tried everything short of the courts.
Letters came first, then a delegation of farmers, then the schoolchildren's choir singing on the company's marble steps.
Through it all the chairman remained obdurate: he received each group courteously, heard the pleas to the end, and refused every one without the smallest change in terms.
Even his own engineers proposed a compromise line that would spare the church and half the orchards; he dismissed it the same afternoon.
Villagers said afterward that arguing with him was like knocking on a sealed door — the knock was always answered, and the door never opened.

obfuscate.definition: Obfuscate means to make something deliberately hard to understand.
obfuscate.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word obfuscate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know obfuscate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The professor accused the textbook of obfuscating: a rule any coach could teach in a minute took the authors nine symbol-choked pages.
Blur is far milder than obfuscate — a blurred explanation softens the edges of one detail, often by accident.
Muddle stops short of obfuscate: a muddled speaker confuses you without meaning to, while an obfuscating one builds the fog on purpose.

Muddy is the informal cousin of obfuscate — stirring silt into water that was clear a moment ago. Anyone can muddy an issue with one careless sentence; to obfuscate is to build the fog deliberately and at length, under jargon and digressions. Muddy belongs to the kitchen table, obfuscate to the courtroom.

To befog is to wrap a subject in mist rather than burying it — the outline stays visible, just softened. Obfuscate goes further: it piles on jargon, digressions, and qualifications until no picture forms at all, and it always accuses the fog-maker of acting on purpose.
clears the fog and shows the thing plainly
state a thing step by step, leaving nothing implied

The root fuscus, 'dark,' arrived in English inside obfuscate and stayed there — no everyday English word shares it. The prefix ob-, 'over, completely,' is everywhere, but the darkness at the heart of this word has no living relatives.
Obfuscate means to make something deliberately hard to understand.

When the collector asked where the atlas had been acquired, the dealer obfuscated — an anecdote about Lisbon, a digression on paper mills, a name that changed twice — until closing time arrived with the question still standing.
Obfuscate is deliberate fog.

Blurring softens a detail, and muddling confuses by accident; to obfuscate is to bury the clear thing on purpose — under jargon, digressions, and qualifications — so that pursuit gives up before it arrives.
Obfuscate is an accusation of intent — it says the fog was manufactured.
Confusing writing may earn 'muddled'; only writing meant to defeat the reader earns obfuscate.
Its unit-mates divide the territory: misrepresent plants a false picture, while obfuscate makes sure no picture forms at all.

Muddy belongs to the kitchen table, obfuscate to the courtroom.

Obfuscate goes further: it piles on jargon, digressions, and qualifications until no picture forms at all, and it always accuses the fog-maker of acting on purpose.

When the city posted its rezoning notice, the residents of Alder Street read all fourteen pages and came away knowing less than they had before.
A retired paralegal in the group suspected that was the point.

The notice, she argued, was written to obfuscate: every plain fact — a warehouse, four stories, overnight truck traffic — arrived buried in cross-references, defined terms, and clauses that pointed to other clauses.
When a reporter asked the planning office to state the project in one sentence, the office declined and cited the document.
The council approved the warehouse eleven days later, before most of the street understood what had been proposed.

oblique.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word oblique. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know oblique should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Tia's oblique postcard said only that the mountains 'ask nothing of anyone,' and the family understood she wasn't coming home soon.
Diplomatic is milder than oblique — the message is softened and cushioned, but it still arrives by the front door.
Veiled goes further than oblique: an oblique remark approaches from the side, while a veiled one hides its meaning almost entirely.

A roundabout answer takes the long way to the point — extra clauses, detours, delay before the meaning arrives. Oblique is about the angle, not the length: a single short oblique line can land its point instantly, just never head-on.

Sidelong is delivered from the side, like a glance you feel rather than meet — it belongs mostly to looks and glances. Oblique reaches further: remarks, criticism, and whole approaches can be oblique, angled away from head-on while still carrying their full message.
aimed straight at the point
open and honest without softening
Oblique is Latin obliquus, 'slanting.' The ob- ('against, aslant') is a familiar prefix, but the -liquus half survives in no other English word, so there is no cousin to peel off.
Oblique means indirect; not straightforward.
The piano teacher never says a performance failed; her oblique verdict — 'the metronome missed you today' — sends students back to the practice room unasked.
Oblique means approaching at a slant instead of head-on: an oblique remark delivers its message while never stating it, leaving the listener to close the last step of the distance.
Oblique praises or accuses indirection, depending on who is speaking — oblique hints, oblique criticism, an oblique approach.
Plain 'indirect' is flatter; oblique adds the sense of an angle chosen on purpose.

Asked directly whether the novel's failed sea captain was based on her father, the author smiled and talked instead about tides.
Her answers all evening were oblique in just that way: never a refusal, never a yes, always a short remark angled off to one side of the question.

Pressed about the book's ending, she said only that 'harbors forgive the ships that miss them.' A less patient interviewer might have called it evasion, but the audience began to hear the answers hiding inside the angles.
By the end, no question had been met head-on, and none, somehow, had gone unanswered.

obliterate.definition: Obliterate means to destroy completely, leaving no trace.
obliterate.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word obliterate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know obliterate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Three laser sessions obliterated the tattoo, and the skin healed so evenly the artist could not say where it had been.
A smudge only blurs the mark — anyone can still see something was there — while obliterate leaves nothing to show anything ever existed.
Erase goes further than smudge — the mark itself comes off the page — but obliterate claims the most: nothing left to show anything was ever there.

To blot out is to cover or soak a mark until it cannot be seen — the ink-and-paper picture obliterate grew from. But a blotted mark is hidden, not gone; lift the cover and traces remain. Obliterate insists that nothing at all survives to find.

Expunge is the official's word: a name or a charge struck from the record, deliberately and by someone with authority. Obliterate is physical and total — shells, lasers, centuries of weather — erasing the thing itself, not just its entry in a file.
to bring it back to what it was
to keep it intact for the future
The one-room school pushed literacy above all else: every farm child reading by eight and writing by nine.
Obliterate means to destroy completely, leaving no trace.

The shelling of 1916 obliterated nine villages around Verdun so completely that when the war ended there was nothing to rebuild — no walls, no wells, not a street line traceable under the leaf litter.
France never rebuilt them.
Each site keeps a signboard in the forest, naming a town that exists now only as a name.
Obliterate is the exact word for what the shelling did, because it means to destroy completely, leaving no trace — and the no trace clause is the whole word.
The Latin beneath it meant to blot out the letters: erasure so total the page forgets the ink.
Damage leaves wreckage to point at; even demolish leaves rubble.
Obliterate leaves absence.
Obliterate is the totality word: reach for it only when nothing is left to point at.

Its unit-mates divide destruction's labor — raze levels a building but leaves the rubble and the lot; eradicate wipes out something living or spreading, to the last case; obliterate erases even the last signs.
If a trace survives, the word has been overspent.

But a blotted mark is hidden, not gone; lift the cover and traces remain.
Obliterate insists that nothing at all survives to find.

When the volcano's mudflow finally stopped, the valley where the village of San Marcos had stood for three centuries was a smooth gray plain.
Archaeologists arrived a decade later expecting buried walls, the way ash had once sealed ancient towns for later discovery.
Instead they found that the boiling lahar had obliterated the site: it had not covered the village but scoured it, dragging stone, timber, and even the street grid down the valley.
Ground-penetrating radar returned nothing; test trenches turned up river gravel where the plaza should have been.
The team's final report was one page long, and its conclusion was blunt: there is nothing here to excavate, because nothing remains.

oblivious.definition: Oblivious means lacking consciousness or awareness of something.
oblivious.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word oblivious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know oblivious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The seagull strutted across the picnic blanket, oblivious to three cats crouched at the garden's edge.
A distracted student misses a sentence when a phone buzzes; oblivious goes further - whole fire drills can pass unnoticed.
An inattentive guard still catches some of what passes the gate; the oblivious one perceives none of it - the word marks total failure to notice.

Unaware is the neutral, no-blame word for simply not knowing, because the information never came your way. Oblivious goes further: the facts are right in front of you — loud, posted, repeated — and your attention still never registers them at all.

Heedless people were warned and pushed on anyway; the word carries blame, because the warning reached them and they paid it no attention. Oblivious carries no such charge — an oblivious person never perceived the warning in the first place.
primed to catch whatever happens next
in the habit of noticing details
Untended, the old orchard slid into oblivion behind the new billboards.
Oblivious means lacking consciousness or awareness of something.
The new dishwasher, headphones snug, scrubbed a single stockpot to a mirror shine for ten straight minutes, oblivious to the ticket printer chattering out orders a foot behind his shoulder.
Oblivious is precise because his awareness simply never registers the printer - no choice, no defiance, just a total failure to notice.
Heedless would accuse him of brushing past a warning he had heard; oblivious says the sound never reached him at all.
Oblivious marks a total failure to notice - often comic, sometimes damning.
It points outward from the person: you are oblivious to the world.
Its mirror in this unit is obscurity, where the world fails to notice you.
Heedless is harsher: the heedless were warned and sailed on anyway.

Oblivious goes further: the facts are right in front of you — loud, posted, repeated — and your attention still never registers them at all.

On the morning the river burst its banks, Elias Grote sat in the window of the Corner Grind, editing a manuscript.
For two hours he was entirely oblivious to the scene beyond the glass: sirens, a loudspeaker truck making passes, neighbors stacking sandbags across the street.
The barista who finally tapped his shoulder said his name three times before he looked up.
'I remember thinking the light had gone strange,' he admitted later.
'I registered nothing else.' He had not chosen to ignore the warnings; as far as his attention was concerned, they had simply never happened.

obscurity.definition: Obscurity means the state of attracting no notice — unknown or forgotten by the wider world.
obscurity.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word obscurity. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know obscurity should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The chess variant spent decades in obscurity before a streaming series made it a lunchtime craze.
Anonymity hides only the name - a donor can stay unnamed while the gift makes headlines; obscurity goes further, leaving the person and the work unknown alike.
Oblivion outdoes obscurity: an obscure poet still sits findable on a library shelf, while a poet in oblivion has vanished from every shelf and every memory.

Namelessness is the plain condition of having no name attached — an unsigned painting, an unmarked grave. Obscurity is wider: an obscure person's name may be perfectly findable, yet nobody looks, because the person and the work alike sit outside the world's notice.

Insignificance means mattering too little to affect anything — small stakes, no consequences either way. Obscurity measures notice, not weight: a discovery can be hugely important and still sit in obscurity for decades, unknown to the wider world until someone finally stumbles onto it.
widely known and talked about
the bright center of public attention

Obscurity is built on Latin obscurus, 'covered over, darkened.' The old covering-root behind -scur- made no other common English word: its only living relatives are obscure and obscurity themselves, so this family tree stops after one branch.
Obscurity means the state of attracting no notice — unknown or forgotten by the wider world.
Most words live and die in obscurity.
'Snollygoster' had its brief career in 1890s newsprint, then sank: no textbook carried it, no speech revived it, and only dictionary editors, turning the yellowed pages, ever met it again.
Obscurity is exact for that sunk-from-view state: the word still exists - a determined reader can find it - but nobody knows it, uses it, or misses it.
Not anonymity (a name kept off known work) and not yet oblivion (erased even from the dictionary): obscurity is the wide, quiet shelf between.
Obscurity names the state of being unknown or forgotten - careers begin in it and often end in it.
Anonymity hides only the name; a person in obscurity is unknown, work and all.
And keep the mirror straight: obscurity means the world overlooks you; oblivious (this unit) means you overlook the world.

In 1957, a Kansas high-school teacher named Ruth Alcott self-published forty copies of a booklet on prime numbers.
It then spent half a century in near-total obscurity: her name was right there on the cover, the booklet sat cataloged in three libraries, and in fifty years the checkout card gathered four stamps.
Nothing was hidden and nothing was secret; the world simply never glanced her way.
When a graduate student finally cited the booklet in 2009, number theorists were startled to find a key result worked out decades early.
Alcott had not been ignored because she was wrong, or concealed, or unimportant -- only unlooked-at.

obstinate.definition: Obstinate means not yielding easily to argument or persuasion; stubbornly set on one's own position.
obstinate.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word obstinate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know obstinate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The obstinate goat would not budge from the garden path, whatever the farmer tried.

Stubborn is the everyday, milder word, and English happily applies it to things as well as people — a stubborn cough, a stubborn jar lid; obstinate is stronger, suggesting a person's determined, unreasonable refusal to yield to actual arguments.
Intractable is stronger than obstinate: an intractable person or problem cannot be managed or steered at all, by anyone.

Headstrong describes someone who charges ahead on their own will, brushing off advice before it is even finished. Obstinate digs in where headstrong rushes forward: the obstinate person refuses to yield to arguments, while the headstrong one refuses to hear them out. One blocks change; the other races past it.

Inflexible means unwilling to bend or adapt — said of rules, schedules, plans, and the people who enforce them without exception. Obstinate is more personal and more willful: an active refusal to yield to arguments and persuasion. A policy can be inflexible; only a mind can be obstinate.
willing to adapt
eager to fit others' wishes
She pedaled the stationary bike by the window while rain streaked the gym glass.
Obstinate means not yielding easily to argument or persuasion; stubbornly set on one's own position.
The debate team had lost three rounds in a row using Lena's opening strategy.
Her teammates showed her the judges' scoresheets and proposed a different order of arguments.
The coach walked her through exactly where the strategy was leaking points.
Lena crossed her arms and announced that the team would open the same way in the final round, too.
Win or lose, she was too obstinate to change course.
Lena refuses to change her chosen course of action despite clear evidence and repeated arguments from everyone around her — that refusal to yield is what makes her obstinate.
neutral-to-disapproving; everyday and formal use
Obstinate is the general-purpose member of this unit's 'stubborn' trio: a broad refusal to change one's mind or course of action.
Obdurate is harsher and more literary, implying a heart hardened against pity itself, while adamant points at emphatic, vocal insistence on one specific point.

Obstinate digs in where headstrong rushes forward: the obstinate person refuses to yield to arguments, while the headstrong one refuses to hear them out.
One blocks change; the other races past it.

Obstinate is more personal and more willful: an active refusal to yield to arguments and persuasion.

Every summer the Ruiz family drove to the coast, and every summer Uncle Tomás insisted on the old canyon road.
This year his nieces showed him the traffic app, his brother printed the new bypass times, and a highway sign itself announced the faster route.
Tomás studied each piece of evidence carefully, nodded at the figures, and remained obstinate, turning onto the canyon road exactly as he had for thirty years.
It was not that he failed to follow the arguments — he could repeat them back perfectly — he simply would not be moved by them.
By August the family had stopped arguing and simply packed extra sandwiches for the long way around.

obstreperous.definition: Obstreperous means noisy and difficult to control.
obstreperous.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word obstreperous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know obstreperous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The obstreperous freshman section drummed the bleachers through both anthems and every whistle.
Fidgety stops far short of obstreperous — fidgeting is squirmy motion, not defiance of the room.
Rowdy stops short of obstreperous — a rowdy crowd is loud in fun, while an obstreperous one is loud against control.

Unruly means refusing to be governed — an unruly class ignores the teacher no matter what the rules say, and it can do so in sullen silence. Obstreperous is unruliness at full volume: the obstreperous drown out whoever is trying to restore order. Unruly can be quiet defiance; obstreperous never is.

Raucous describes the sound itself — harsh, grating, ear-filling noise, whatever its purpose. Obstreperous is about the noise's target: an obstreperous crowd aims its racket against whoever is trying to bring it to order. A raucous gull colony is merely deafening; an obstreperous classroom is deafening at its teacher.
quietly submissive, giving no trouble at all
simply making little noise

The heart of this word is Latin strepere, 'to make a racket' — a wonderfully noisy verb that left no other descendants in everyday English. You may recognize the prefix ob- ('against') from words like object, but the racket in obstreperous is all its own; learn the word whole.
Obstreperous means noisy and difficult to control.

Halfway through the estate auction, the back row turned obstreperous—bidding by air horn, shouting over the auctioneer's patter, rattling the folding chairs—until the gavel came down and the lot was withdrawn entirely.
Obstreperous adds defiance to volume: a loud room is merely noisy, but an obstreperous one is noisy against whoever is trying to run it—it resists being brought to order.
Obstreperous suits crowds, children, and animals who are loud and fighting control — often with a raised eyebrow of humor.
Plain 'rowdy' covers cheerful noise; reserve obstreperous for noise aimed at whoever is trying to restore order.
Its unit-mate querulous is the opposite volume of trouble: a stream of whiny complaints rather than a roar.

Eighteenth-century London managers did not fear a bored audience; they feared an obstreperous one.
When the Theatre Royal tried to raise ticket prices in 1763, playgoers did not write letters.

The management posted notices begging for order; the notices were read aloud from the pit in funny voices, to cheers.

obtuse.definition: Obtuse means slow to understand or catch on.
obtuse.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word obtuse. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know obtuse should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The sitcom runs on an obtuse landlord who hears 'the ceiling leaks' as small talk about weather.
Distracted misses the hint only because attention is elsewhere — call the name and the point lands fine — while the obtuse listener is looking right at you and still takes the long way in.
Impenetrable goes further than obtuse — the obtuse listener gets there late; with an impenetrable one, the hint never arrives at all.

Slow-witted is the plain insult: it blames the wits themselves, claiming the whole mind runs slowly — arithmetic, directions, jokes, all of it. Obtuse is narrower and a shade kinder: the obtuse person can be brilliant elsewhere while hints, irony, and subtext take the long way in.

Thick-headed is the schoolyard picture — a wall the message bounces off, blunt and jeering. Obtuse says nearly the same thing in adult, written English, and it alone carries the accusation of pretending: telling someone not to be obtuse means you suspect they understand perfectly well.
the signal lands before the sentence ends
the all-purpose opposite: edges intact

Latin tundere, 'to beat,' left English almost nothing you'd meet at dinner — its other descendant is contusion, the medical word for a bruise, which you'll meet later in this course. For building new words, this root is a dead end.
Obtuse means slow to understand or catch on.
For a week the interns assumed Bo was joking.
Told the fire drill was 'a dress rehearsal,' he asked where the costumes were kept; handed a box marked THIS SIDE UP upside down, he rotated the sticker toward himself and kept walking.
He isn't careless — he's obtuse: hints, irony, and arrows all land a beat late.
Obtuse is the exact word because it means slow to perceive or understand — the signal arrives and takes the long way in.
Geometry uses the same word for the angle past ninety degrees — the corner worn round — and that's the picture: not a missing mind, but an edge rounded off.
Obtuse criticizes uptake — hints, warnings, and subtext bouncing off.
Keep it apart from its unit-mate facile: the obtuse listener can't see the point; the facile thinker sees one instantly and digs no further.
And 'don't be obtuse' accuses someone of pretending not to understand — the word's most common live use.

For two weeks the whole office worked around Dev.
The party planning happened in plain sight, because Dev had a reputation for being magnificently obtuse about hints.
Colleagues asked what cake he liked 'for a cousin's birthday.' They borrowed his guest list 'for a seating study.' He answered every question helpfully and suspected nothing.
It was not that his mind was slow.

Decorations may blanket a room; each carved rosette is an ornament.
adornment: An adornment is a decorative touch that beautifies something, and the word leans toward what is worn or draped — jewels, garlands, embroidery.
An ornament is a free-standing decorative object in its own right, often part of a building or display.
A necklace is an adornment; the carved rosette above a door is an ornament.
trinket: A trinket is a small, showy object of little practical value — the kind of thing collected on a shelf or won at a fair.
An ornament can be finely made and genuinely treasured; what defines it is being added purely for beauty.
A trinket is cheap by definition; an ornament need not be.
eyesore: something ugly and unpleasant to look at
blemish: a mark or flaw that spoils an appearance
accent → ornament → showpiece

ornament: A showpiece goes beyond an ornament — it's the star attraction, meant to impress everyone who enters the room.
When the city rebuilt the Fourth Street bridge, the plans were all girders and load limits — except for one odd line item: four cast-iron pelicans, one for each corner post.
The pelicans held nothing up.
They carried no wire, shaded no walkway, and cost eleven thousand dollars the auditors tried twice to cut.
The chief engineer defended them in a single sentence: a bridge people love is a bridge people maintain.
Each pelican is an ornament in the strict sense — an object with no job except to please the eye of whoever crosses.
Sixty years on, the girders have been replaced twice, but when one pelican cracked in a storm, the city recast it within a month, from the original mold.

oscillate.definition: Oscillate means to swing back and forth between two positions or states.
oscillate.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word oscillate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know oscillate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The desk lamp hung from the tent pole and oscillated with every gust, swinging its shadow from one wall to the other.
Quiver is milder than oscillate — a quivering needle trembles around one spot, while an oscillating one sweeps the whole dial between its two ends.
Careen is stronger than oscillate — an oscillating swing is regular and bounded, but something careening slings itself about with no rhythm and no fixed stops.

Swing is the plain word for moving to and fro — a gate can swing once and stop, and nothing fixes where it goes. Oscillate is stricter: it requires two set poles and a repeated return trip between them, often on a rhythm steady enough to time.

To shuttle is to travel back and forth between two places, like a ferry or an airport bus, and the word stays physical — bodies and vehicles shuttle. Oscillate covers the same two-pole round trip but reaches further: needles, voltages, moods, and undecided minds all oscillate.
to come to rest at one position and stay
to keep moving steadily in a single direction

The swinging little oscillum stayed a one-word family: outside oscillate and its own offspring, oscillation and oscillator, the root built nothing else in English. Meet oscill- and you are always looking at the same swinging mask.
Oscillate means to swing back and forth between two positions or states.
The broken thermostat made the office oscillate between sauna and icebox — twenty minutes of roasting, a clank from the vents, twenty of shivering, and back, all winter long.
Oscillate needs exactly two poles: back and forth, A to B and home again, often on a rhythm you could set a watch by.
Movement that wanders with no fixed endpoints is mere fluctuation; the pendulum, the metronome, and the undecided mind all oscillate because they keep returning to the same two stations.
Oscillate is precise: two poles and a return trip, often on a rhythm.
Engineers give it to circuits and pendulums; writers borrow it for moods and negotiations that keep swinging between the same two states.
For an undecided person specifically, vacillate — a word you met earlier in this course — stresses the indecision; oscillate stresses the motion.

When the new footbridge opened, the design team stayed behind to watch it under load.
By mid-morning, with commuters crossing in step, the deck began to oscillate: it leaned a hand's width toward the east rail, then the west, then east again, on a beat you could count.
A junior engineer timed it.
The trip from one extreme to the other took just under two seconds, and the deck repeated the trip without variation.
'It isn't drifting and it isn't shaking at random,' she wrote in the log.
'It travels between the same two limits, over and over.' Dampers went in that week, and the deck's steady two-ended motion faded to an occasional shiver.

ossify.definition: Ossify means to become rigid and stop changing.
ossify.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word ossify. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know ossify should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The chef worried that the menu had begun to ossify: the 'seasonal specials' had not changed in four years.
Habits can harden and still be broken with effort; hardening is the milder, earlier stage of what ossify completes.
Fossilize goes further than ossify: the ossified rulebook still runs the club, while the fossilized one survives only as a curiosity from another age.

Calcify means to stiffen with mineral deposits, and figuratively to grow inflexible. It is ossify's near-twin — one image from lime, one from bone — and like ossify it describes something still standing and still in force, just no longer able to bend.

Stagnate means to stop moving or developing, like still water going stale. A stagnant committee produces nothing new but could still change course; to ossify is to harden past the point where change is possible. Stagnation is idleness; ossifying is rigidity.
to change to fit new conditions
to keep developing over time

Latin os, 'bone,' survives in English almost nowhere outside the anatomy lab — ossuary, a chamber for storing bones, is its rare other descendant — so there is no everyday relative to lean on. The familiar half is the suffix: -ify, 'to make,' the same maker that builds mollify, vilify, and stupefy in this unit.
Ossify means to become rigid and stop changing.
Grandpa's morning route had ossified decades ago — the same bench, the same crossword, the same two slices of rye — and the family learned that even a new toaster counted as an upheaval.
Ossify is literally 'to turn to bone,' and the figurative sense keeps that image: habits, institutions, or opinions that were once living and flexible harden until they cannot bend without breaking.
Ossify is the pointed choice for institutions, rules, and thinking that have stopped being able to change — it diagnoses, where 'harden' merely describes.
Its unit-mate mollify makes a neat opposite pair to remember: one word softens, the other turns to bone.

The academy's fencing curriculum was once the envy of Europe, revised yearly as masters returned from tournaments with new footwork.
Somewhere in the last century the revisions stopped, and the syllabus began to ossify.
The forms are still taught in strict order, the examinations still enforced to the letter; nothing has been abandoned, and nothing can be touched.
When a young instructor proposed adding a single modern parry, the committee did not reject the idea so much as fail to locate any procedure by which an idea could be considered.
Visitors sometimes mistake the stillness for decline, but the school is thriving by every measure it recognizes — enrollment is full, the drills immaculate, the year 1911 preserved in amber.

ostensible.definition: Ostensible means stated as a reason, but not necessarily the real one.
ostensible.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word ostensible. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know ostensible should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her ostensible reason for the 6 a.m. run was training; the bakery along the route told the fuller story.
A declared purpose is simply the one on paper, no wink attached; ostensible raises the eyebrow.
A sham goes past ostensible: ostensible leaves room for the stated reason to be true, while a sham reason is false outright — a costume over the real one.

Professed means declared aloud by the person concerned — a professed pacifist has said so herself, believe it or not. The word points at the act of announcing. Ostensible points at the gap between the reason shown and the reason held, and needs no announcement at all — only a surface.

Purported passes along someone else's claim with a visible shrug — a purported Rembrandt is called that secondhand, by tellers who will not vouch for it. Ostensible is the observer's own cooler verdict on a stated reason: here is the version on display; the truth may sit elsewhere.
the real thing
what is truly so
You met ostentatious in Course 1: even the marina's oldest members found the new arrival's yacht ostentatious.
Ostensible means stated as a reason, but not necessarily the real one.
Her ostensible reason for the 6 a.m.
run was training; the bakery along the route told the fuller story.
The dean announced that the new sign-in sheet outside the studio was about fire safety — an ostensible purpose nobody openly doubted.
But the sheet appeared the same week the kilns began emptying overnight, and the only column anyone ever checked was who had been in the building after ten.
Ostensible neither accuses nor clears: it marks the gap between the reason shown and the reason held.
Ostendere, 'to show,' does the work — the ostensible motive is the one held up for viewing.
If you know the show is false, sham or pretended says so; ostensible keeps the question politely open.
Ostensible is the reporter's raised eyebrow: it marks the reason shown without ruling on the reason held.
Softer than sham, which convicts, and cooler than supposed, which smirks, it suits filings, motives, and agendas — anywhere the show and the truth might differ.

In April the parks department closed Miller's Pond for what a laminated sign at the gate called habitat restoration, promising the return of nesting turtles.
That was the ostensible reason, and the town newsletter repeated it without comment.
The budget told a different story.
Winter storms had cracked the pond's retaining wall, and the repair estimate ran to eighty thousand dollars the department did not have.
No turtle survey was ever filed.
The restoration contractor listed on the permit turned out to specialize in concrete work.
When the pond reopened two years later, the wall was new, the ledger was balanced, and the sign about turtles was quietly gone.

ostracism.definition: Ostracism means exclusion from a group by deliberate shunning.
ostracism.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word ostracism. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know ostracism should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: New hires who skipped the union picnic learned that a season of quiet ostracism could be colder than any reprimand.
A snub is a single icy moment — one greeting refused, one invitation withheld; ostracism is that treatment organized and sustained by the whole group.
Banishment goes further than ostracism: the group does not merely freeze you out of its company, it formally casts you out of the place itself.

Exclusion is the broadest term for being left out — by rule, by chance, or by design, once or always. Ostracism is one specific kind: deliberate, sustained shunning by a group of one of its own, enforced through cold behavior rather than any written rule.

Shunning is the pointed avoidance itself — the turned backs, the unreturned greetings — and a single person can shun another. Ostracism is that treatment organized and sustained: a whole group closing ranks against one member and keeping the freeze going for weeks.
being taken in as one of the group
the warm reception an outsider hopes for
The reef's oysters clamp their shells shut the instant a shadow passes over the bed.
Ostracism means exclusion from a group by deliberate shunning.
Naturalists describe ostracism among ravens: a bird that steals from the shared cache is driven to the edge of the roost, and for weeks none of the others will feed beside it.
Ostracism is more specific than rejection because it is exclusion enforced by the group's own behavior — no ruling, no announcement, just a closing of ranks that leaves one member outside them.
Ostracism is the analyst's word for group-enforced exclusion — sociable animals, playgrounds, and office floors all practice it.
It needs no official act; the freeze itself is the punishment.
Pariah, taught in this unit, names the person on the receiving end: ostracism is the treatment, a pariah is its target.
For one cold incident, snub or slight is enough.
