resolute: Determined says you truly intend to do it; resolute goes further - the decision is settled, and pressure will not reopen it.
resolute: Immovable outdoes resolute: the resolute negotiator holds her position through every argument, while an immovable one will not even return to the table to hear a new offer.
Imani Sesay moved the marsh orchid into a different genus, half the botanical world objected within a month.
Journal editors hinted at retraction, conference panels were arranged to rebut her, and a senior rival wrote three open letters.
Sesay stayed resolute: she had spent nine seasons in the field before deciding, and she declined to reopen the question under pressure.
Asked whether anything could change her mind, she answered that a new specimen could - a louder letter could not.
Two independent genetic studies later confirmed the reclassification, and the letters quietly stopped.

resonate.definition: Resonate means to stir a deep and lasting sense of connection.
resonate.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word resonate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know resonate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The night-shift nurse never guessed a picture book about moving day would resonate so with her young patients; three families have asked to keep the copy.
To appeal is a fainter thing than to resonate — a poster can appeal to you and be forgotten by dinner.
Haunt goes further than resonate: what resonates keeps meaning something to you, while what haunts you follows you into quiet moments uninvited.

To strike a chord is to connect at once with someone's feelings — the phrase names the instant of recognition, the nod in the moment. To resonate asks what happens afterward: the connection must run deep and keep lasting. Plenty of ads strike a chord on first viewing; far fewer still resonate a month later.

To ring true is to feel accurate to your own experience — a matter of believability, the detail that sounds exactly right. To resonate goes past accuracy into attachment: the thing stirs a deep and lasting connection. A crime drama can ring true without moving anyone; what resonates keeps mattering after the credits.

The jet crossed the coast with a sonic boom that set off car alarms for a mile.
Resonate means to stir a deep and lasting sense of connection.

The documentary's quietest scene — a father re-lacing his daughter's skates with numb fingers — resonates far beyond hockey towns: months later, it is the moment reviewers name when asked what stayed with them.
Resonate means to stir a connection that is deep and lasting, not merely to please.
The test is time: what resonates keeps returning — quoted, remembered, felt again — long after the applause has faded.
An image can delight for an evening; the one that resonates follows you home.

Two years later, the letters are still the most visited room in the building.
Visitors do not just skim and move on.
They stand a long time at a 1907 note in which a father apologizes for missing his daughter's first word, and many return with their own children.
The director thinks she knows why the letters resonate: they name a cost — distance from the people you love — that has not changed in a century.
The guest book bears her out.
The most common entry, in a dozen languages, is some version of 'this is my family too.'

respite.definition: Respite means a short period of rest or relief from something difficult.
respite.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word respite. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know respite should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The ceasefire gave the border villages a two-week respite, long enough to bring in the harvest.
A breather is seconds or minutes snatched mid-effort; respite goes further — a real stretch of relief in which the pressure genuinely lifts.
Deliverance goes far beyond respite: a respite ends and the hardship returns, while deliverance means being rescued from it once and for all.

A reprieve is relief that someone with power grants — the execution stayed, the deadline pushed back, the closure postponed. It comes down from a decision. A respite needs no one's signature: the shelling pauses, the fever breaks, the pain lets up. Both are temporary; only a reprieve is issued.

A lull is a quiet spell in the activity itself — the wind drops, the shelling thins, the orders stop coming in. It is measured from outside and need not be felt as relief by anyone. A respite is defined by the sufferer: relief from hardship, felt as relief, with the hardship waiting.
a sustained attack or flood of demands
unrelenting, wearing work
The rookie earned the crew's respect one careful weld at a time.
Respite means a short period of rest or relief from something difficult.
When the monsoon finally paused, the road crews got a five-day respite: time to patch the washouts, shore up the hillside, and sleep past dawn for the first time in a month.
Nobody mistook it for the end of the rains — the second front was already on the forecast.

Respite is more exact than break because it requires hardship on both sides of it: a coffee break interrupts an ordinary morning, but a respite is carved out of something genuinely punishing, and everyone knows the punishment resumes.
Respite needs hardship to push against: heat, grief, shelling, double shifts.
For a pause with nothing painful around it, break or lull is the honest word.
Its cluster-mate repose is the resting itself — during a respite from the grind, you might finally repose.

For two years Lena's alarm had gone off every three hours, around the clock, so she could check on her father.
When her aunt flew in for ten days and took over the night shifts, Lena did not know what to do with the silence at first.
She slept, then slept more.
She saw a film in a theater.
She read forty pages of a paperback without listening for footsteps.
The whole visit, she knew, was a respite and not a rescue: the flight home was already booked, and the alarm would return to her nightstand.
But relief that is temporary, her aunt insisted, is still relief — and Lena flew through her days like proof.

resplendent.definition: Resplendent means dazzlingly splendid; gloriously bright.
resplendent.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word resplendent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know resplendent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The peacock fanned its tail and stood resplendent, a hundred green-gold eyes catching the sun.
Bright is plain light, far below resplendent — a hallway bulb manages bright, with no majesty anywhere in it.
Gleaming goes further than bright — surfaces polished until they flash — but it stops short of resplendent, which adds majesty to the shine: a whole presence lit up in glory.

Dazzling is light-first — anything bright enough can dazzle, from a welder's arc to headlights on high beam, and the word says nothing about grandeur. Resplendent asks for more: the eye must be overwhelmed and honored at once, with majesty riding on the light.

Magnificent means grand — by size, cost, or sheer ambition — and it needs no shine at all. Resplendent is narrower: reserved for visual glory, where light and majesty arrive together, so a thing must actually blaze before resplendent fits it.
dull, colorless, beneath notice
grimy and dim with wear
Reviewers called the aurora splendid, and crowds drove north all winter to see it.
Resplendent means dazzlingly splendid; gloriously bright.
The tall ship came up the channel for the festival resplendent: full sail set, forty signal flags snapping from her rigging, brass rails flashing, her bow carvings freshly leafed in gold.
Traffic stopped on the bluff road.
Children who had never cared about boats pointed and yelled.
She was, for one morning, the only thing worth looking at on that water.
Resplendent is the exact word for the ship that morning, because it means dazzlingly splendid, gloriously bright — light and majesty arriving together.
Dazzling alone could describe a welder's arc; resplendent insists the eye is overwhelmed and honored at once.
Resplendent is reserved for visual glory — light plus majesty.

Dazzling can describe any bright thing and magnificent any grand one; resplendent insists the eye is overwhelmed and honored at once, which is why it gravitates to ceremonies, plumage, treasure, and skies.
No unit-mate competes for its lane; just remember the re- is an intensifier, not 'again' — the word promises shining through and through, never shining twice.

For sixty years the Alhambra Theater sat dark, its chandelier crated in the basement and its gilded balconies painted over in gray.
The restoration crew worked from photographs taken on opening night, 1912, peeling the gray away to find gold leaf underneath.
On the night of the reopening, the chandelier rose to the dome on its original winch and its four hundred crystals caught the stage lights all at once.
A critic wrote that the old house was not merely bright again but resplendent: the light itself seemed ceremonial, as though the room had put on robes.
Ticket holders reportedly stopped in the doorway, unwilling to walk in and interrupt it.

restitution.definition: Restitution means restoration of something lost, or compensation paid for a loss or injury.
restitution.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word restitution. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know restitution should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The judge ordered the con artist to pay full restitution to the retirees whose savings he had drained.
A refund is weaker than restitution, a refund simply returns the price you paid, while restitution makes up for the full loss a person actually suffered.
Reparations are stronger than restitution, restitution repays one victim for a specific loss, while reparations attempt to compensate entire groups for large-scale harm.

Compensation is any payment made to make up for a loss, injury, or inconvenience — insurance payouts, damages, even overtime pay. Restitution is the pointed version: restoring to a specific victim what they lost, or its full value, typically because the payer is answerable for the loss.

Repayment means giving back what is owed — settling a loan or a debt you took on. The money was always due. Restitution answers a loss rather than a debt: something was taken or destroyed, and its value is restored to the person who suffered the loss.

Redress is a remedy that sets a wrong right, and it can take almost any form — an apology, a policy change, a payment. Restitution is one specific kind of redress: restoring what was lost, or paying its value, to the person who was harmed.
officially seizing someone's property
the taking away or withholding of something needed
The city council voted to institute curbside recycling across every neighborhood by next spring.
Restitution means restoration of something lost, or compensation paid for a loss or injury.
After Theo accidentally knocked over and shattered Mrs.
Bell's antique porch lamp, he mowed her lawn every week that summer as restitution.
Theo cannot un-break the lamp, so he makes up for the loss with work of equal value.
Providing something to compensate for what another person lost is precisely what restitution means.
Most at home in courtrooms and formal writing, in collocations like pay restitution, make restitution, and restitution to the victims.
Do not confuse it with the sound-alike retribution, which means punishment or revenge; restitution repays a loss, while retribution inflicts one in return.

The community greenhouse on Alder Street was wrecked one October night: panes shattered, seed trays overturned, a season's work of the gardening club undone in an hour.
When two teenagers were caught on camera, the club asked the juvenile court for something other than jail.
The judge agreed and ordered full restitution: the pair would pay for every broken pane out of their own wages and rebuild the cedar benches they had kicked apart.
A donated check from a sympathetic stranger was declined; the club insisted the cost fall to the two who caused the loss.
By spring the glass was back, the benches stood again, and the ledger of the loss was closed by the people answerable for it.

restive.definition: Restive means restless and impatient under restraint, straining against control or delay while still being held in check.
restive.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word restive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know restive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The colts grew restive in the starting gate as the third false start was announced.
Impatient is weaker than restive: an impatient person merely wants the wait to end, while a restive one is visibly beginning to strain against whatever is holding things up.
Mutinous is stronger than restive — a mutinous crowd is on the edge of open revolt, while a restive one is still contained, just barely and unhappily.

Fidgety means unable to stay still — tapping, shifting, checking the clock — restless energy with no particular target. Restive gives that energy a grievance: restless impatience straining against the specific restraint or delay causing it. A fidgety child squirms anywhere; a restive one squirms against the seatbelt.

Uneasy means unsettled and vaguely anxious, a discomfort that may have no clear cause at all. Restive is sharper and points outward: restless impatience straining against a known restraint or delay. An uneasy audience worries quietly; a restive one starts pushing at whatever holds it.
able to wait calmly
calm and at rest
A stationary bike stands in place no matter how hard you pedal — from stare, 'to stand,' the same standing-still root hiding inside restive.
Restive means restless and impatient under restraint, straining against control or delay while still being held in check.
The documentary crew had promised the villagers a ten-minute ceremony before filming began.
An hour later, cables still snaked across the square and the director kept calling for one more lighting check.
Children broke from their parents to chase pigeons; two elders stood and stretched pointedly; a low murmur ran through the rows of folding chairs.
The longer the delay stretched, the more restive the crowd became — not angry yet, but visibly done with waiting.
The murmuring, pointed stretching, and children drifting off show a crowd growing restless and resistant under an imposed delay — the exact condition restive names.
formal; journalistic (crowds, legislatures, animals)

Restive describes impatience under restraint or delay — a held crowd, a waiting horse, a stalled legislature — which distinguishes it from this unit's combative: a restive group strains against being made to wait, while a combative one is actively spoiling for a fight or argument.

The storm pinned Halley Research Station shut for nine straight days, and the safety officer's rule was absolute: nobody stepped outside.
By the sixth day the crew had grown openly restive.
The delay itself was bearable; the order holding them indoors was what they strained against.
Two glaciologists demanded a waiver to check their instruments.
A cook was found half-suited in the airlock, arguing that the wind had dropped.
The station manager wrote in her log that the mood was not boredom.
It was pressure against a rule, rising a little with every hour the rule held.
When the wind finally eased on day nine, the door opened to a line of people already dressed, packed, and pushing to be first through it.

reticent.definition: Reticent means hesitant to speak up; keeping one's thoughts to oneself.
reticent.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word reticent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know reticent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Grandpa stayed reticent about his years at sea; asked directly, he would nod at the horizon and change the subject.
Private is milder than reticent — a few doors politely closed, plenty still shared — while the reticent keep most of their thoughts unspoken as a general habit.
Walled-off goes further than reticent — a reticent colleague still answers when pressed, while a walled-off one lets nothing through at all.

Tight-lipped is the informal twin of reticent, and it usually clamps shut on one subject in particular — the coach goes tight-lipped about the starting lineup. Reticent describes a person's whole manner: answers short, opinions unoffered, on most topics and most days.

Guarded adds wariness to the quiet — a guarded speaker weighs every word for risk, protecting something from listeners who might use it. Reticent needs no threat at all: the silence is a comfortable preference, chosen and kept even among people who are trusted.
the chatter flows freely on any topic
offers information before being pressed

Reticent grows from Latin tacere, 'to be silent' — a root English did keep, in tacit (understood without being said) and taciturn (silent by temperament), both taught elsewhere in this course. This card leaves them to their own lessons; notice only that re- adds no repetition here — just silence, thorough and chosen.
Reticent means hesitant to speak up; keeping one's thoughts to oneself.

Three lunches into her first week, all anyone at the workshop knew about Imani was that she kept bees — and that only because a jar of honey had appeared on the break table with a small handwritten label.
Reticent but warm, she answered questions briefly, asked better ones back, and returned to her sandwich.
The crew liked her enormously and knew almost nothing about her.
Reticent is the exact word for Imani, because it means hesitant to speak up, keeping one's thoughts to oneself — the silence is chosen, comfortable, and aimed mostly at her own affairs.
Guarded would imply wariness, something protected; reticence needs no threat at all, only a preference.
Reticent describes people, and their manner, when thoughts stay unspoken: answers short, opinions unoffered.
Tight-lipped is the informal twin, usually about one topic; guarded adds wariness.

Two boundaries matter: reluctant — a cousin in this unit's reference list — is unwillingness to act, while reticence is unwillingness to speak; and recalcitrant, this unit's louder mate, refuses authority outright.
The reticent refuse nothing; they simply are not saying.

When Priya was assigned Marcus Chen as a lab partner, she assumed his silence meant he resented the pairing.
He answered questions in five words or fewer, offered no opinions about anything -- music, professors, the weather -- and ate lunch with a book.
Halfway through the term she noticed the pattern: he was exactly the same with his oldest friends, and none of them seemed to mind.
Marcus was simply reticent, their TA explained -- not hostile, not hiding anything, just built to keep most of his thoughts to himself.
When he finally did volunteer a full sentence -- that her titration technique was the best in the section -- Priya framed the compliment.

retract.definition: Retract means to withdraw a statement, promise, or claim, especially because it was found to be wrong.
retract.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word retract. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know retract should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The newspaper had to retract its front-page report once documents proved the local factory had actually passed its safety inspection.
To qualify a statement is weaker — you soften it or add conditions while still standing behind it, instead of retracting it outright.
To abjure is stronger — it is a solemn, often sworn renouncing of a belief entirely, going beyond retracting one mistaken statement.

Withdraw means to pull back or take back something offered or stated — a bid, an application, a remark — and it is the general word for any pulling-back. Retract is the pointed version: you take back a specific public statement or claim because it proved wrong. You can withdraw an offer that was perfectly sound; a retraction admits error.

Rescind means to officially cancel a decision, offer, or rule — a company rescinds a job offer, a board rescinds a policy. What gets rescinded is an act with legal or official force. Retract applies to things said or published: statements, claims, and testimony taken back as mistaken.

Recant means to formally give up a belief or position one once professed, classically under pressure — heretics were made to recant. Retract is narrower and factual: you take back a particular statement or claim because it turned out to be wrong, with no change of creed required.
to state firmly that something is true
to continue insisting that a claim is correct
The buzzing phone kept trying to distract Jonah from the practice test.
Retract means to withdraw a statement, promise, or claim, especially because it was found to be wrong.
After an outside team found a critical error in the lab's measurements, the chemist chose to retract the paper rather than defend a flawed result.

Retract fits because the chemist is formally taking back a published claim — the paper — specifically because it was discovered to be wrong, which is the word's core situation in science and publishing.
Retract is the standard word in journalism, science, and law — newspapers retract stories, researchers retract papers, witnesses retract testimony.
It also keeps its literal 'pull back' sense (a cat retracts its claws).
In casual conversation, people usually say 'take back' instead.

In her acclaimed history of the Aldwyn shipyard, Dr.
Ferris wrote that the company had hidden a 1911 fire from its investors.
The claim was repeated in reviews, quoted in documentaries, and taught in at least one university course.
Then a graduate student located the shipyard's original ledger, which showed the fire had been reported to investors within a week.
Ferris did not hesitate: in the next printing she moved to retract the claim, and the publisher inserted a note calling the passage an error.
Colleagues praised the correction; as one put it, a historian's authority rests less on never erring than on what she does when the record proves her wrong.

retrospective.definition: Retrospective means looking back on or dealing with past events and situations.
retrospective.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word retrospective. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know retrospective should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The clinic's retrospective review of five years of patient charts revealed which treatments had actually helped.
Reminiscent is gentler than retrospective — usually something is reminiscent of the past, evoking a few memories in passing, while a retrospective review deliberately examines a whole stretch of it.
Elegiac is more intense than retrospective — an elegiac poem doesn't just look back at what happened, it openly mourns what is gone.

Backward-looking means focused on the past, and it often carries a sniff of criticism — a backward-looking policy resists whatever comes next. Retrospective is neutral and deliberate: a retrospective review examines the past on purpose to learn from it. Backward-looking is an orientation; retrospective is an activity.

Reflective means thoughtfully reviewing what has happened — a quiet, musing frame of mind a person falls into. Retrospective is more structured: it names a deliberate look back across a defined stretch of the past, like a report or exhibit. A person feels reflective; a review is retrospective.

Nostalgic means feeling a bittersweet, affectionate longing for a past time — it names an emotion. Retrospective is cool and workmanlike: a retrospective report examines the past without necessarily missing it at all. Nostalgic is how looking back can feel; retrospective names the act of reviewing.
focused on the future
concerned with what is to come
After the tournament, Dana stayed quiet and introspective for the rest of the weekend.
Retrospective means looking back on or dealing with past events and situations.
In a retrospective essay for the paper's final issue, the graduating editor looked back on four years of late-night deadlines and hard-won lessons.
The essay examines events that already happened — four years of the editor's own past — which is precisely what makes it retrospective.
This course teaches retrospective as an adjective ('a retrospective report,' 'a retrospective glance').
You may also meet it as a noun — 'a retrospective' is an exhibit reviewing an artist's whole career.
Watch the near-twin retroactive: a retroactive rule reaches back to take effect from a past date, while something retrospective looks back to examine the past.
Reviewing versus rule-changing — keep them separate.

Retrospective is neutral and deliberate: a retrospective review examines the past on purpose to learn from it.

Rangers pulled old collar data, weather logs, and the notebooks of biologists long since retired.
The final report praised some early choices and flagged others that had nearly sunk the effort in its third winter.
Nobody involved called the work sentimental; it was an audit of the past, done on purpose, to guide the next release.

revel.definition: Revel means to enjoy something with unrestrained, exuberant enthusiasm — often used as 'revel in.'
revel.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word revel. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know revel should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The whole third grade reveled in the surprise snow day, sledding until their mittens froze solid.
To enjoy something is simply to take pleasure in it; to revel in it is to enjoy it loudly, freely, and without holding anything back.
To carouse goes past reveling — boisterous merrymaking stretched into a long, noisy spree.

To bask is to soak quietly in a pleasant glow that comes from outside you — praise, good news, sunshine — the way a cat lies in a warm patch of light. To revel is the loud opposite: enjoyment with every restraint thrown off. Basking is still and content; reveling climbs onto the furniture.

To luxuriate is to sink into comfort or pleasure and stretch it out at length, self-indulgently, like staying in a hot bath after the water cools. To revel is more public and more explosive — unrestrained celebration rather than slow, private indulgence. You luxuriate at leisure; you revel out loud.
to sulk in gloomy silence
to feel deep sorrow
A rebellion is an uprising against authority — the same Latin root rebellare that hides inside revel, where the only thing overthrown is restraint.

They dragged the prop couch to the middle of the stage, blasted the show's soundtrack, reenacted every flubbed line at triple speed, and danced in their costumes until the janitor flicked the lights.
After eleven weeks of rehearsal, they had earned the right to revel — and they held nothing back.
The blasting music, wild reenactments, and dancing until lights-out show enjoyment with all restraint thrown off — that unrestrained abandon is what it means to revel.

reverent.definition: Reverent means showing deep, awed respect — treating something as near-sacred in how you speak, move, or stay silent before it.
reverent.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word reverent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know reverent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The apprentice lifted the old luthier's violin with reverent care, as though a careless breath could crack it.
Respectful is milder than reverent: a respectful visitor follows the rules and keeps a polite tone, while a reverent one is quieted by genuine awe.
Worshipful goes further than reverent — reverent respect keeps a human distance, while worshipful devotion treats its object as divine.

Respectful is the everyday, all-purpose word — polite and considerate toward anyone, in any setting — and it asks nothing more of you than good manners. Reverent goes much further: the respect deepens into awe, is saved for what feels close to sacred, and shows in hushed voices and careful hands.

Solemn describes the weight of a mood or occasion — grave, formal, no lightness anywhere — without pointing at anything. Reverent is aimed: deep respect directed at one particular thing held in awe. A judge can be solemn all day out of habit; a person is reverent only before something.
treating what deserves seriousness as a joke
looking down on it with open contempt
Sixty years on, the village still addresses its letters to Reverend Achebe, though the old chapel has been a library for decades.
Reverent means showing deep, awed respect — treating something as near-sacred in how you speak, move, or stay silent before it.

No sign at the trailhead asks for quiet, and none is needed: a dozen paces into the grove of two-thousand-year-old redwoods, the loudest tour group of the morning went reverent all at once — voices dropped mid-sentence, footsteps slowed, and one hiker reached out to touch the bark, then let his hand fall without making contact, as if the tree had a right to refuse.
Reverent is the exact word for that hush, because it means showing deep, awed respect — treating something as near-sacred in how you speak, move, or stay silent before it.
Nobody instructed the group; the awe did.
A respectful group would have kept the trail rules and the noise down, and thought no more about it; a reverent one lowers its voice the way people do in front of something they cannot quite measure.
formal / solemn, warmly positive
Reverent belongs to the one offering the respect, never to the thing receiving it: the pilgrims are reverent, the shrine they walk to is revered.

Keep its neighbors straight — respectful is everyday courtesy with no awe in it; solemn is gravity of mood that points at nothing in particular; reverent is respect deepened into awe and aimed at something held near-sacred.
Two traps ride along with this word: the sound-alike reverie is a daydream, no relation at all, and the re- up front is an intensifier — a reverent hush is not a hush that happens again.

Hikers take off their hats without being asked, and voices drop to the level of a library, or lower.

The grove has no guards and no fences, she points out, and in twenty years no one has carved so much as an initial.

revise.definition: Revise means to reconsider and make changes to something, especially a written work, in order to improve it.
revise.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word revise. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know revise should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: After reading the judges' comments, Tomás stayed up late to revise his competition essay, cutting the weak opening and adding stronger evidence.
To tweak a draft is to make one or two tiny adjustments — far lighter than to revise it, which means rethinking the whole piece to improve it.
To overhaul a draft goes further than to revise it: you tear it down and rebuild it from the ground up.

Rework means to shape the material again from a fresh angle — a scene rebuilt around a different character, an essay reorganized around a new thesis. Revise is wider and calmer: reconsider the work and change whatever needs improving, large or small. All reworking is revising; much revising is gentler than reworking.

Amend means to alter something formally, usually to correct or improve it — laws, contracts, and official records are amended. Revise belongs to drafts and working texts: a writer reconsiders and changes their own pages to make them better. Parliaments amend a bill; writers revise a chapter.

Polish means to refine the small details until the writing shines — smoothing sentences, sharpening word choices, perfecting what already works. Revise can cut far deeper: reconsidering structure, arguments, and whole passages. Polishing is the finishing touch at the end; revising can rebuild the middle of the work.
to keep exactly as written, without changes
to leave something untouched and unimproved
The head baker stayed late to supervise the new apprentices in the kitchen.
Revise means to reconsider and make changes to something, especially a written work, in order to improve it.

The playwright spent the whole summer working to revise her second act: she reconsidered every scene, cut a character who slowed the story, and rewrote the ending twice before the script finally felt right.
She didn't just reread the act — she reconsidered it and made changes to improve it.
That combination of looking again and changing for the better is the heart of revise.
neutral, school and publishing
Revise is the standard word for improving a draft, and its related noun form is revision — both the act of revising and the changed draft itself.
One caution: in British English, revise can also mean to study for an exam; the SAT tests the 'rework a text to improve it' sense.

Some notes were small — a date wrong, a clumsy phrase.
Others were structural: the middle section buried the announcement the whole speech existed to make.

She cut the history lesson from the middle, moved the announcement to the second minute, and rewrote the ending to point at it.

revitalize.definition: Revitalize means to bring new energy and strength back to something that has slowly grown weak, dull, or inactive.
revitalize.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word revitalize. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know revitalize should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Hoping to revitalize the diner's tired menu, the new chef added a dozen colorful dishes that soon had regulars lining up out the door again.
Refresh is weaker than revitalize; a cold drink refreshes you for a moment, but it does not give something whole new life.
Resurrect is stronger than revitalize; you revitalize something that is fading, but you resurrect something that is completely gone.

Rejuvenate means to make something feel young and fresh again — a spa weekend rejuvenates you, a redesign rejuvenates a brand. It restores a youthful feel. Revitalize restores working energy and strength: a revitalized downtown has businesses and foot traffic again, not just a fresher look.

Reinvigorate means to put new vigor into something flagging — a pep talk reinvigorates a tired team. It usually boosts effort, morale, or momentum. Revitalize runs deeper and slower: it brings a fading place, institution, or enterprise back to real strength and life.

Revive means to bring something back from having stopped — a canceled tradition can be revived, and so can a person who has lost consciousness. Revitalize needs no full stop: it pumps fresh energy into something that still exists but has gone flat, like a tired menu or a declining downtown.
to drain completely of energy
to make dull or lifeless
The old dog surprised everyone with the vitality of a puppy the moment the leash came off the hook.
Revitalize means to bring new energy and strength back to something that has slowly grown weak, dull, or inactive.
After weeks of drought, a single night of steady rain revitalized the tomato garden, and by morning the drooping vines stood tall and green again.
The vines had grown weak and droopy, and the rain gave them back their strength and liveliness overnight.
Bringing fresh life and energy to something that was fading is exactly what revitalize means.
Common in news writing about places and institutions: people revitalize a downtown, an economy, or a career.
Do not confuse it with revive, which often means bringing someone back to consciousness; revitalize means pumping fresh energy into something that still exists but has gone flat.

For years the Saturday farmers' market in Lindenvale had been shrinking: a dozen stalls where sixty once stood, and vendors who packed up by noon.
The market never closed outright -- a few growers always came -- but everyone agreed it had gone flat.

She recruited young farms from three counties and gave each a season's stall for free.

Two summers later the lot was full again, and the market pulsed with an energy old-timers said they had not felt in twenty years, though its wooden stalls and hand-painted signs were the same ones as ever.

revoke.definition: Revoke means to officially cancel a right, privilege, or official document, often as a consequence or punishment.
revoke.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word revoke. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know revoke should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: After the third safety violation in one month, the city moved to revoke the factory's operating permit.
Suspend is weaker than revoke: a suspended license is only paused and can come back, while a revoked license is canceled outright.
Strip is stronger than revoke: revoking takes back one specific privilege, while stripping someone of their rights takes away nearly everything at once.

Withdraw means to take back something that was granted or put forward — a company withdraws a job offer, a diplomat withdraws a proposal — and it implies no wrongdoing. Revoke is punitive and official: an authority cancels a specific right, privilege, or document as a consequence of misconduct. Anyone can withdraw for any reason; revoking answers a violation.

Cancel is the all-purpose word for officially calling off or ending something — a meeting, a subscription, an order. Revoke is narrower and harsher: an authority takes back a granted right, privilege, or official document, usually as punishment. Anything can be canceled; only something granted can be revoked, and usually for cause.
to restore something that was taken away
to officially give a right or privilege
Whenever chores came up, Dad would solemnly invoke a family rule that nobody could remember agreeing to.
Revoke means to officially cancel a right, privilege, or official document, often as a consequence or punishment.
The state medical board gave Dr.
Hale two written warnings about falsifying patient records.
When an audit uncovered a third violation, the board finally acted: it voted to revoke his medical license.
The decision was a direct consequence of his misconduct, and it took away the one specific privilege his career depended on.
From that day forward, he could no longer legally practice medicine anywhere in the state.
The board canceled a specific professional privilege as a punishment for wrongdoing, which is precisely what revoke means.

For years the valley's most popular radio station promised listeners that its call-in contests were open to anyone with a phone.
Then a former producer revealed that the biggest prizes had gone, week after week, to friends of the owner reading from scripts.
The broadcasting commission held hearings, documented the rigged contests, and concluded that the station had abused the public's airwaves.
Its response was the harshest tool it had: it moved to revoke the station's broadcast license as a punishment for the deception, and the frequency went silent at midnight.
The owner may apply again in five years, the commission noted, but nothing obliges it to say yes — the license he held is gone, not resting.

rhapsodize.definition: Rhapsodize means to engage in excessive enthusiasm.
rhapsodize.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word rhapsodize. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know rhapsodize should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Get Grandpa started on his old orchard and he will rhapsodize until the porch light comes on.
To mention a thing is to spend one sentence on it and move on — the far, quiet end of this scale; rhapsodizing lives at the other end entirely.
To enthuse is real, audible excitement, but rhapsodizing is stronger and longer than enthusing — praise settling in for the evening, with imagery.

To gush is to spill over-eager praise in one quick burst — a splash of superlatives, then done. To rhapsodize is longer-winded and more elaborate: the praise builds images and settles in. A gush is over in a breath; rhapsodizing wants the whole evening.

To rave is to praise at top volume — wild, emphatic, and brief enough that a critic can rave in a single sentence. To rhapsodize trades volume for altitude and length: image after image, praise that unspools. A rave is a shout; a rhapsody is a recital.
to say deliberately less than you feel
low, unimpressed muttering
For homework she wrote an ode to the school's vending machine, rhyming 'quarters' with 'headquarters.'
Rhapsodize means to engage in excessive enthusiasm.
Our sommelier began to rhapsodize about the '09 vintage — comparing it to a cello, then to October, then to a small cathedral — while the soup went quietly cold.
To rhapsodize is to praise at length and altitude — talk that has left the ground and doesn't want to land.
It is intransitive: you rhapsodize about or over something.
The gusher enjoys it more than the listener, which is the word's gentle joke.
Rhapsodize gently teases while it praises: it says the speaker's enthusiasm has become a performance.
Use it for the friend who cannot stop describing the ramen.
Gush is quicker and wetter; rave is louder; extol (in this unit's reference list) is the sober, formal cousin — you extol to persuade a committee, you rhapsodize because you can't help it.

rhetorical.definition: Rhetorical means relating to the art of persuasive speaking or writing; (of a question) asked for effect, not expecting an answer.
rhetorical.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word rhetorical. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know rhetorical should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: At the debate-team workshop, students marked every rhetorical device in the famous speech, from its unanswered questions to its drumbeat of repeated phrases.
Polished speech is simply well-finished; rhetorical speech deliberately deploys the tools of persuasion.
Bombastic language inflates rhetorical technique into overblown, self-important noise.

Oratorical relates to formal public speaking as a whole — the delivery, the podium manner, the grand occasion. Rhetorical points at the persuasive craft inside the speaking: the devices and strategies designed to move an audience. A booming voice is an oratorical gift; a well-placed repeated phrase is a rhetorical one.

Stylistic covers any feature of how something is written or said — sentence length, tone, word choice — with no particular aim attached. Rhetorical names the features aimed specifically at persuading an audience. A fondness for semicolons is stylistic; a drumbeat of repeated phrases built to sway listeners is rhetorical.

Unanswerable describes a question no one can answer — too hard, or without any answer to give. A rhetorical question could be answered easily; it simply is not meant to be, because it exists for effect. The unanswerable question defeats replies; the rhetorical question never wanted one.
A genuine question truly seeks information; a rhetorical one expects no answer at all.
Plainspoken delivery skips crafted devices entirely and just says things straight.
Ancient Athens paid handsomely for lessons from a famous rhetorician.
Rhetorical means relating to the art of persuasive speaking or writing; (of a question) asked for effect, not expecting an answer.
Okada asked the class, 'Do we really want to be the group that gives up before the experiment even starts?', the question was rhetorical—he was already handing out the lab goggles.
No answer is expected; the question exists purely for effect, to rally the class.
That is the classic rhetorical question.
The word can also describe anything relating to the craft of persuasive speaking or writing itself.
academic; everyday in the fixed phrase 'rhetorical question'
In essays and criticism, rhetorical describes the craft of persuasion—rhetorical devices, rhetorical strategies.
In everyday speech it lives almost entirely in the phrase 'rhetorical question,' one asked for effect with no answer expected.
Note that calling something rhetorical says nothing about whether it actually convinces anyone—that would be persuasive.

On Nia's first day at the paper, the opinion editor handed her a marked-up editorial about the failing water system.
Every circle flagged a rhetorical move: the question that expected no answer, the tripled phrase 'test it, fix it, fund it,' the deliberate echo of the city's own slogan turned back on the council.
'None of this is decoration,' the editor said.
'Each device exists to push the reader toward one conclusion — that the council must act.' Nia noticed what was not circled: the paper's habitual short paragraphs, its plain vocabulary.
'House manner,' the editor shrugged.
'That part persuades no one.' By the third draft of her own first editorial, Nia was counting her circles before anyone else could.

ribald.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word ribald. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know ribald should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The retirement roast turned ribald by the second toast, and the honoree's grandchildren were steered early to the dessert table.
Naughty is milder than ribald — a wink of mischief that stays fit for the greeting-card aisle.
Obscene is harsher than ribald: ribald humor works blue for laughs, while the obscene has crossed the line whether anyone laughs or not.

Bawdy means cheerfully indecent in the tavern-song tradition — good-natured, winking, meant for a room that wants to laugh. Ribald covers the same blue territory but runs coarser and more daring: a bawdy verse teases, while ribald humor barrels past the line grinning. Both live or die by the joke.

Earthy means frank about bodies and appetites in a natural, unembarrassed way — a farmer's bluntness rather than a dirty joke. Ribald turns that frankness into comedy and pushes it toward the indecent on purpose. Earthy talk need not be funny or crude at all; ribald must be both.
carefully proper and easily scandalized

ritualized.definition: Ritualized means turned into a fixed form repeated the same way each time.

In the morning it voted to sanction the Riga open — official approval that puts the tournament on the world calendar and makes its results count for ratings.
In the afternoon it turned to discipline: a grandmaster caught consulting a hidden phone mid-game.
The measure it imposed was harsher than any caution — a two-year ban from rated play and forfeiture of his prize money, imposed under the federation's anti-cheating rules.
Delegates joked that a newcomer reading the minutes would need a glossary: the same body had spent one day approving a tournament and penalizing a cheater, wielding one word both ways.

sanguine.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word sanguine. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know sanguine should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Down three games to one, the manager stayed oddly sanguine, penciling in the same lineup and predicting a comeback by Sunday.
Wishful is wanting without expecting — milder than sanguine, which genuinely believes the good news is coming.
Blithe goes further than sanguine — the sanguine planner expects things to work out and still checks the forecast; the blithe one has stopped checking anything at all.

Hopeful means wanting and wishing for the good outcome — hope reaches for good news but stops short of forecasting it. Sanguine goes further and expects: cheerful, settled confidence that things will come right. Hope crosses its fingers; sanguine checks the calendar and smiles.

Confident means sure of the outcome — certainty, with or without a smile. Sanguine adds the good cheer and makes the whole outlook a temperament: a sanguine person meets bad news still cheerfully expecting things to come right. You can be grimly confident; nobody is grimly sanguine.
expecting the worst, and glum about it
convinced the bad outcome is the likely one

Latin sanguis, 'blood,' built almost nothing else you'd meet in an ordinary English day — its other descendants (sanguinary, consanguinity) are rare legal and literary visitors. Learn sanguine on its own, and let the four-humors story hold it in memory.
Sanguine means optimistic, cheery.
The startup's servers crashed on launch morning, but its founder stayed sanguine on the all-hands call: 'We patch tonight, we relaunch Friday, and in a year this is the story we tell at parties.'
Sanguine is optimism as a temperament — confident good cheer that holds up in bad weather.
Hopeful people want the good outcome; sanguine people expect it.
Medieval doctors thought the mood came from a healthy supply of blood, and the word still carries that ruddy, unbothered glow.
Sanguine is the polished word for durable optimism — analysts are sanguine about earnings, captains stay sanguine in storms.
It is steadier than upbeat (in this unit's reference list) and roomier than hopeful: hope wants, sanguine expects.
In this unit's weather system, sanguine is the climate while elated is a single sunny burst.

It was arithmetic: eleven years of weather logs said the window would open, and she expected exactly that.
Thursday dawned windless and blue.
By seven the team was on the ridge.

sanitize.definition: Sanitize means to make something thoroughly clean and free of germs.
sanitize.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word sanitize. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know sanitize should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Wipe-down stations let members sanitize each bench and bar before the next lifter steps up.
Tidying up is far weaker than sanitizing: it only puts things where they belong and leaves the germs untouched, while sanitizing scrubs a surface until the germs themselves are gone.
Clean handles what the eye can see — crumbs and dust are gone — but it stops short of sanitizing, which goes after the germs you cannot see.
Sterilize goes further than sanitize — sanitizing knocks germs down to safe levels, while sterilizing kills every last organism, lab-style.

To disinfect is to kill germs with a chemical agent — the sprays and wipes of the cleaning aisle name the weapon. Sanitize names the standard instead: a surface is sanitized once its germs are down to safe levels, however you got there. You disinfect with something; you sanitize to a level.

To cleanse is to clean something deeply and thoroughly — skin, a wound, even a reputation — with no particular promise about germs. Sanitize makes exactly that promise: not just clean, but germ-safe. A cleansed counter looks and feels spotless; a sanitized one has been made safe to eat from.

sardonic.definition: Sardonic means grimly mocking and scornful — humor with dark disdain running underneath it.
sardonic.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word sardonic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know sardonic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The tow-truck driver kept a sardonic sign bolted above the winch — 'Your shortcut, my salary' — and waved pleasantly at every car in the ditch.
Wry is milder than sardonic — a small, crooked smile at life's ironies, affectionate as often as not, with none of sardonic's scorn.
Sneering goes further than sardonic: the humor drains away entirely and open contempt is all that's left on the face.

Mocking is the broad word for making fun of something, from playground teasing to open ridicule — the mockery can even be affectionate. Sardonic is mockery served cold: the laugh has scorn in it, and the speaker sounds half-finished with the world he's laughing at.

Cynical describes a belief — that people act from self-interest and every promise is for sale. Sardonic is what that belief sounds like when it smiles: the dry, dark joke a cynic makes instead of an argument.
sincere and serious, meaning every word straight
amused in a warm way, with no scorn in the laugh

The trail behind sardonic dead-ends in legend: Greek sardonios was tied — by story, not by sound law — to Sardinia and its face-twisting plant, and the root built nothing else in English. There is no everyday cousin to reuse; the word stands alone, smirking.
Sardonic means grimly mocking and scornful — humor with dark disdain running underneath it.
After the third round of budget cuts, the lab director's memos turned sardonic: 'Good news — headquarters believes we can cure the disease with two beakers and the interns' optimism.'

Sardonic is more precise than 'sarcastic' because sarcasm is a technique — saying the opposite of what you mean — while sardonic names the temperature: cold, scornful amusement, usually aimed at fate, folly, or the whole absurd situation.
A sardonic speaker isn't erupting in anger; the joke is how little he expects anymore.
Sardonic is the reviewer's word for humor that scorns what it describes — a sardonic narrator, a sardonic aside.
Two unit-mates patrol the same block: acerbic stings with a sour, witty bite, and vitriolic has stopped joking altogether.
Sardonic is the coolest of the three — it mocks darkly and keeps its seat.

satiate.definition: Satiate means to satisfy fully or to excess.
satiate.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word satiate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know satiate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The tasting portions were tiny on purpose: the chef wanted guests intrigued, not satiated, when the main course arrived.

Glut goes further than satiate — to satiate is to fill completely; to glut is to stuff past all pleasure, into queasy excess.

Sate is the blunt old sibling of satiate — to fill someone completely, full stop. Satiate does the same work in a longer robe, and it more readily tips past fullness into too much: a sated guest is done eating; a satiated one may be groaning.

Quench answers thirst specifically — water on a fire, the drink that puts wanting out. Satiate answers hunger and appetite in the broad sense: for food, novelty, or success, filling the want completely until nothing more is asked.

satirical.definition: Satirical means using humor, irony, or exaggeration to criticize or mock foolishness.
satirical.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word satirical. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know satirical should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The late-night show's satirical sketch "thanked" smartphone makers for finally freeing families from the burden of dinner conversation.
Playful teasing amuses without any real target; satirical humor aims its jokes at a genuine flaw.
Scathing criticism burns without needing jokes at all—harsher than satirical wit.

Mocking covers any ridicule at all — a sneer, a cruel imitation, a scornful laugh — with no method required. Satirical ridicule works through humor and clever overstatement, and it aims at a real flaw worth exposing. All satire mocks; most mocking has none of satire's craft or purpose.

Tongue-in-cheek describes playful insincerity — saying what you don't quite mean, with a wink, purely for fun. Satirical work borrows that wink and points it at a target: the humor exists to criticize a real foolishness. A tongue-in-cheek toast teases; a satirical sketch indicts.

Sardonic names a tone — scornful, biting, darkly amused — that can color a single remark and needs no purpose beyond itself. Satirical names a project: using humor, irony, or exaggeration to expose a real flaw. A sardonic aside mocks the moment; satirical work is built around its target.
Earnest expression means every word sincerely, with no hidden mockery.
Reverent treatment honors its subject rather than poking fun at it.
By Friday the rain had saturated the practice fields, and the game was moved indoors.

scant.definition: Scant means barely sufficient — so little that it falls short of what is needed.
scant.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word scant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know scant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The detective had only scant evidence: a single blurry footprint by the gate.
A slim supply is small but might still stretch far enough; a scant supply falls short of what's actually needed.
Scant evidence is at least some evidence; nonexistent evidence is none at all.

Minimal means the least possible amount, often pared down on purpose — minimal packaging, minimal fuss. It suggests a floor deliberately reached. Scant is about accident and shortfall: less than the situation needs, with nobody choosing it. A minimal design succeeds by using little; scant evidence fails by having little.

Negligible means so small it hardly counts and can safely be ignored — a negligible fee, a negligible risk. Scant amounts still count; they are just not enough. Scant attention is real attention that falls short of what is needed; negligible attention might as well be none.

Slight means small in degree — a slight delay, a slight accent, a slight improvement — measuring how far something departs from zero or from normal. Scant measures against need: scant evidence, scant hope, scant regard are amounts that fall short of what the moment requires.

scathing.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word scathing. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know scathing should be able to work it out from your sentence.

scintillating.definition: Scintillating means sparkling with quick, dancing points of light — and, of lively talk or wit, flashing with the same brilliance.
scintillating.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word scintillating. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know scintillating should be able to work it out from your sentence.

Sparkling is the everyday twin — quick points of light dancing off water, glass, or lively talk. Scintillating means the same motion with more polish and more voltage: the sparks come thick and fast, and the word itself dresses up, especially for brilliant conversation. Glittering is hard, bright flashing — sequins, frost, a case of diamonds — and it can feel cold or even suspect, as in glittering prizes. Scintillating keeps the flash but warms it with life and wit. scrupulous.definition: Scrupulous means painstakingly careful and honest.
scrupulous.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word scrupulous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know scrupulous should be able to work it out from your sentence.

A simplified account has been honestly trimmed for its audience; a simplistic one trimmed away truths the audience needed.
Cartoonish goes past simplistic — so squashed that even its author couldn't mistake it for the real thing.

Reductive names the method: boiling a complex thing down until the meaning distorts — history as a single cause, a person as a single trait. Simplistic names the verdict on the result: the account now treats the matter as simpler than it truly is. Reductive is how it happened; simplistic is what it became.

Oversimplified is the plain-English twin: an account simplified past the point of truth. Simplistic says the same thing in the critic's register and reaches further — an oversimplified summary may have gone too far by haste, while simplistic can also indict the thinking behind it as shallow from the start.
alive to fine distinctions
keeps the full stack of causes in view
Harbor pilots apprentice for years before anyone trusts them to read the bay's complex currents.
Simplistic means treating a complex matter as simpler than it really is.
The subway map and the consultant's one-page picture of the company hang side by side in the lobby, and they fail differently.
The map strips away streets, hills, and true distances, and keeps every connection that matters: honest simplicity.
The picture is simplistic: it draws the company as five clean boxes reporting neatly upward — and the dotted lines where decisions actually travel appear nowhere.
Employees laughed for a week.
Simplistic is the exact word for that picture because it treats a complex matter as simpler than it really is — simplification past the point of truth.
That's the whole difference between simple and simplistic: simple shed the clutter and kept the truth; simplistic shed some truth to get the tidiness.
One is a virtue of style, the other a defect of thought.
Simplistic is always an accusation — it says the simplifying went too far and cost the truth.
Never use it to praise ease; that job belongs to simple.

Its unit-mates divide the territory: inane says a remark had no content to begin with, fatuous adds smug delight, while simplistic grants that the content exists — and objects that the hard parts were shaved off.
Reductive is its close ally.

When the lake turned green in July, a flyer went up in the marina: 'It's the geese.
Chase off the geese and the water clears.' The harbor board liked the flyer.
Geese were visible, countable, and easy to blame.
The county's water scientist called the theory simplistic.
Yes, geese add waste — but so do lawn fertilizer, a failing sewer main, and a summer with no rain to flush the shallows.
Treating a four-cause problem as a one-goose problem, she warned, meant the lake would stay green no matter how many birds were chased away.
The board funded the goose patrol anyway.
In August the water was greener than ever.

simulate.definition: Simulate means to reproduce the appearance or workings of something — to produce a convincing stand-in for the real thing without being it.
simulate.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word simulate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know simulate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The hoverfly cannot sting, but its yellow-and-black bands simulate a wasp so convincingly that birds give it the same wide berth.
Mimic is lighter than simulate: a mimic copies the look or sound of a thing in the moment, while simulating rebuilds its whole behavior — conditions, responses, and all.
Counterfeit goes further than simulate: a simulation is openly an imitation, but a counterfeit is built to be taken for the genuine article — imitation pushed all the way into fraud.

To mimic is to copy the look or sound of something in the moment — a comedian mimics a senator's drawl, a lyrebird mimics a chainsaw. To simulate is to rebuild the thing's whole behavior: conditions, responses, consequences, usually so they can be studied or practiced.

To replicate is to produce an exact duplicate — the same experiment, the same result, the same object again. To simulate is to produce a convincing stand-in: the flight never leaves the ground, and nobody needs it to, because behaving like the real thing is the entire job.
to face the real event itself, stakes and all
to create something new rather than model the real
Before email, wire photos and page proofs traveled by facsimile machine — the fax — curling out of the roller one warm sheet at a time.
Simulate means to reproduce the appearance or workings of something — to produce a convincing stand-in for the real thing without being it.

Before the crew ever touches the real spacecraft, they log four hundred hours in a mock-up that simulates it down to the switch guards — the cabin tilts, the instruments fail on cue, and the windows play footage of the turning Earth.
The mock-up is not a spacecraft and never pretends to leave the ground.
To simulate is to reproduce the conditions and behavior of the real thing so faithfully that practice inside the copy transfers to the original — imitation built for use, not for deceit.
Simulate is morally neutral machinery: flight crews, economists, and epidemiologists all simulate, and nobody blames them, because a simulation announces itself as an imitation.

The deception words in this unit begin exactly where that announcement stops — feign is a person faking their own state, counterfeit is imitation built to be taken for the genuine article, and legerdemain hides the imitation altogether.

On Tuesday afternoons, the medical school's east ward admits twelve patients who are not sick.

They are trained actors, and the ward exists to simulate the worst hour of a residency: one 'patient' seizing, another quietly slipping into shock, a third demanding a diagnosis at the top of his voice.
Monitors display vitals scripted in a control room; the crash cart is stocked; the clock is real.
Students know none of it is genuine and sweat anyway, because the ward reproduces how an emergency behaves — its pacing, its noise, its decisions — without ever putting a life at risk.
Errors made on Tuesday, the dean likes to say, are the cheapest ones the hospital sells.

sinuous.definition: Sinuous means winding and curving in a graceful, snake-like way.
sinuous.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word sinuous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know sinuous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: From the canyon rim the river below looked like a sinuous ribbon of silver, folding back on itself again and again.
Curved describes a single bend, while sinuous means the bending repeats, one graceful turn after another.
Serpentine is the most vivid word in the group: it insists on the image of a snake in motion, while sinuous can describe any smoothly winding shape.

Winding says a road or river bends repeatedly along its length, and it is neutral about how those bends look or feel. Sinuous is winding with grace added: smooth, continuous, snake-like curving, which is why it flatters whatever it describes.

Meandering describes a slow, lazy wandering from side to side, named for a winding river, and it hints at aimlessness -- a meandering speech loses its listeners. Sinuous keeps the repeated curves but adds grace and purpose, with nothing lazy about the line.
running without any bend at all
going from one point to another by the shortest line
Within a week the new intern had managed to insinuate herself into the planning committee's lunches.
Sinuous means winding and curving in a graceful, snake-like way.
The old post road between the two valley towns covers nine kilometres as the crow flies, yet drivers travel twenty-six kilometres getting from one to the other.
The road never runs straight for more than a hundred metres: it swings left around a rock spur, curves right along a stream, and doubles back on itself twice near the summit.
Tour buses are banned because they cannot follow the bends.
Cyclists love the road for exactly that reason, since its sinuous course makes every kilometre a new turn.

Twenty-six kilometres of continuous bends to cover nine kilometres of straight-line distance, with no stretch straight for more than a hundred metres, is precisely the smooth, snake-like winding that sinuous describes.
descriptive; usually admiring

Sinuous is a compliment more often than not, since it suggests grace in the curving, which is why it suits rivers, dancers, and coastlines but sounds odd applied to something merely crooked or damaged.
Keep it for smooth, continuous curves: a path that turns in sharp right angles is angular or zigzagging, not sinuous.

Photographs of the Great Wall usually flatten it into a straight line, but no one who walks it remembers it that way.
The wall is sinuous: it pours along the ridgelines in smooth, continuous curves, bending with every fold of the mountains rather than cutting through them.
Its builders had no choice.
A defensive wall must hold the high ground, and the high ground of northern China goes nowhere in a straight line.
From a watchtower the result can look almost alive, a grey line curving out of one valley and into the next until haze swallows it.
Hikers say the grace is deceptive: what flows like a ribbon from a distance is a stiff climb underfoot.

sobriety.definition: Sobriety means calm, grave seriousness of manner.
sobriety.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word sobriety. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know sobriety should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Even the class clown read his half of the war diary with sudden sobriety.
Seriousness only says the joking has stopped; sobriety goes further, adding calm weight and self-command to the manner.
Grimness goes past sobriety into darkness: the sober speaker is grave but steady, while the grim one has let bleakness into her voice.

Gravity is the felt weight of a matter or a manner — the room registers that something serious is underway, and the situation itself can have it. Sobriety belongs to a person's bearing and adds self-command: calm, unhurried, clear-headed. A crisis has gravity; the leader who meets it steadily shows sobriety.

Solemnity is gravity dressed for ceremony — the hush of a funeral, an oath, a state occasion — dignity performed in ritual form. Sobriety needs no occasion at all: it is one person's grave, composed manner, as much at home in a weather briefing as at a memorial.
lightness or joking where weight is expected
bubbling, unserious excitement
The quarterly numbers made for sobering reading in the boardroom.
Sobriety means calm, grave seriousness of manner.
Four hundred meters below the summit, the expedition leader gathered the climbers and spread the weather charts on the snow.
She cracked none of her usual jokes and rushed no one; she laid out the numbers, named the risks, and asked each climber in turn.
Her sobriety told them more than the forecast did — they voted to turn back.
Sobriety is stronger than seriousness because it adds weight and composure: she is not merely unjoking but unhurried, calm, and equal to the gravity of the decision.
Note the word's other everyday sense — not being drunk — which context alone rules out here.
Sobriety names a manner: calm, grave, weighed.
Because it also commonly means not being drunk, let context do the disambiguating — 'the sobriety of the eulogy' is safe, 'his sobriety' alone may mislead.
Its cluster-mate stoic faces inward at hardship endured without complaint; sobriety faces outward, the gravity an audience can see.

The harbor pilots of Punta Arenas board other people's ships in some of the worst water in the world, climbing rope ladders in the dark to steer vessels they have never touched through the Strait of Magellan.
Captains remember the moment a pilot takes the bridge.
The wind may be screaming, but the pilot speaks quietly, asks for coffee, and studies the charts as if the night were calm.
One veteran, Elena Vidal, is famous for her sobriety in the strait's narrowest passage: orders given in a low, even voice, no wasted words, hands folded behind her back.
Crews say the manner is contagious.
Panic, one captain wrote, cannot survive ten minutes of watching her.
The strait stays as dangerous as ever.
What changes, when a pilot like Vidal is aboard, is the temperature of the people facing it.

solipsistic.definition: Solipsistic means treating one's own mind or self as the only thing that truly exists or matters.
solipsistic.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word solipsistic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know solipsistic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The band's documentary is oddly solipsistic — three of the four members appear only as elbows at the edge of the drummer's close-ups.
Self-absorbed people sink into their own concerns but can be pulled back out — the mildest rung, well below solipsistic.
Egocentric goes further than self-absorbed — every event measured by its effect on me — yet it still stops short of solipsistic, which quietly doubts the rest of you are fully there at all.

Self-centered people put their own needs and comfort first — the best seat, the last word, the bigger share. Solipsistic goes past grabbing into attention itself: the solipsistic speaker takes nothing from anyone; other people simply never come into focus as quite real.

Narcissistic means in love with your own image and hungry for admirers — the mirror, the applause, the follower count. Solipsistic needs no admirers, because it has forgotten the audience exists. A narcissist performs for the crowd; the solipsist no longer notices there is one.
tuned to what someone else is feeling — a word from this unit's own list
attention aimed at the world beyond the self
Her first solo album took three years and four studios to finish.
Solipsistic means treating one's own mind or self as the only thing that truly exists or matters.
The captain's log from the disastrous voyage is notoriously solipsistic: the reef, the storm, and the mutinous crew each appear only as obstacles standing between the captain and his breakfast.
Solipsistic is more precise than 'selfish' because selfishness is about hoarding advantages; solipsism is about attention — behaving as if no mind but yours is quite real.
The solipsistic writer isn't cruel to other people; other people simply never come into focus.
Solipsistic is the heavyweight complaint about self-focus — reviews and essays use it when a work treats the world as scenery for one mind.
For garden-variety self-focus, 'self-centered' is honest and shorter.
Its unit-mate sophomoric mocks a different flaw: the sophomoric performer shows off badly for an audience; the solipsistic one has forgotten the audience exists.

Every measurement began and ended with Vail.
Counters sat at the height of his elbows, and the single reading chair faced away from the door.
Visitors noticed what was missing.
There was no guest room, no second chair, not even a coat hook that a caller might use.
Asked about it, Vail seemed genuinely puzzled.
Other people, one interviewer wrote, 'appeared never to have entered his calculations at all.' Admirers of the house praise its honesty.
Its critics answer that a home built as if no one else existed teaches a lesson no one should want.

soluble.definition: Soluble means able to dissolve in a liquid.
soluble.task: Write one sentence of your own using the word soluble. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know soluble should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Washable-marker ink is soluble by design, which is why the art smock survives the school year.

Flour is mixable — beaten through water it makes a cloudy suspension, and by morning it has settled back out; soluble goes further than mixable: the solid truly disappears into the liquid and stays gone.
Instant goes past soluble — a plain soluble powder still wants a stir and a little patience; an instant one is engineered to vanish the moment it lands in the liquid.

Dissolvable says only that a thing can be dissolved — the plain, do-it-yourself word. Soluble is the term chemistry and labels prefer, the one that comes with conditions attached: soluble in what, at what temperature, how completely.

Dispersible means breaking into particles fine enough to spread evenly through a liquid without truly dissolving — the near-miss printed on medicine labels. Soluble goes the whole way: the solid passes into the liquid itself, invisibly, and stays gone.
stays solid no matter how long the stirring goes on
made to shed liquid entirely — waterproof ink is exactly the ink that will not wash away
Dissolve adds dis- (apart): to loosen a solid apart into a liquid, sugar into tea.
Soluble means able to dissolve in a liquid.
Rock candy begins with a fact children refuse to believe: sugar is so soluble that half a kilo will disappear into a single cup of near-boiling water.
The syrup looks like nothing.

Then a string goes in, the jar sits on a shelf, and for two weeks the trick runs backward — as the water cools and departs, the sugar has nowhere to stay, and it climbs out of hiding one glittering crystal at a time.
Soluble is the exact word for the sugar, because it means able to dissolve in a liquid — to break up into particles too small to see and vanish evenly into it.
The property belongs to the solid: sugar is soluble in water the way iron is not, and the whole candy trick is just that ability, lent and then taken back.

Soluble describes the solid that vanishes; this unit's solvent names the liquid that swallows it — keep the pair pointed in opposite directions, since a chemistry answer that swaps them is wrong twice.
Labels lean on soluble (water-soluble vitamins, soluble aspirin); in looser prose a soluble problem is one that can be solved, the same Latin loosening applied to a knot of a different kind.
